items.title: Should an admission ever carry prior incidents? `priorIncidents` is hard-coded to 0 and nothing decides whether it should be
items.body:
Found while implementing #535 decision 5. Measured, not inferred, and re-run at both ends of a varied sentence range.

## What was measured

Every admission the HUD can make sends `priorIncidents: 0` — it is hard-coded beside the sentence in `src/main.ts`'s `ADMISSION_REQUEST`.

With `priorIncidents` at 0, the **reachable classification tiers are `[0, 1]`**. `classificationGroupIdForTier` only answers `'high-risk'` at **tier 3**.

So: **no admission a player can make has ever produced a high-risk prisoner.** `room.solitary-cell`'s accommodation branch is reachable only through a later classification review, never through the front door.

## Why this matters more than it looks

It is not one dead room. Classification tier decides **cell sharing, contraband introduction and the regime timetable** — so the entire high-risk half of three separate systems has never been exercised by ordinary play.

It also explains a finding from a different agent, arrived at independently the same afternoon: a playtest built two furnished `room.solitary-cell` instances, ran an assault on day 8, and could not determine whether anyone was ever sent to solitary. On this evidence, they could not have been.

And it lands beside #538 — where five prisoners sat at Cell Assignment for four in-game days while two empty solitary cells stood next to them. Those cells could not have taken them, because nobody admitted through the HUD is ever high-risk.

## Deliberately not fixed in the branch that found it

`agent/sentence-length-variation` left `priorIncidents` at 0 on three grounds, all of which hold:

- #535 decision 5 is about **sentences**, not priors, and widening a change past its decision is how scope rot starts.
- Tiers decide cell sharing, contraband and the timetable, so moving them is a **balance** change with reach well beyond intake.
- Holding `priorIncidents` at 0 is exactly what bought that change its bit-identical-tiers property: every classification outcome of every existing seed is unmoved, measured across `tests/determinism/` (175 passed, every canonical state hash in `session-replay.test.ts` unchanged).

That was the right call. Filed separately so it gets its own decision rather than riding along on one it does not belong to.

## The decision this needs

Whether an admission should ever carry priors, and if so how they are chosen, is **balance and therefore the owner's**. Three shapes worth distinguishing before choosing:

1. Priors are drawn, like the sentence now is — every prison eventually receives high-risk arrivals.
2. Priors stay 0 and high-risk is reachable **only** through in-play conduct — the current design, made deliberate and stated, with the consequence accepted that a fresh prison's first prisoners are never high-risk.
3. The player chooses at intake — most control, most new interface, and it needs its own answer on whether a high-risk arrival pays more.

If (2) is chosen, then whether a classification review actually fires often enough to reach tier 3 in ordinary play becomes the next thing to measure — nobody has seen it happen.

items.title: [Construction] Removing a built object dismantles it into salvage that must be carried to a storeroom
items.body:
Owner decision. Removing an object is not a delete — it is a **dismantle**, and what comes out of it has to be **carried to a storeroom**. It does not evaporate, and it does not teleport back into the builder's hands.

This is the mirror image of the purchase→delivery loop decided in #96. Goods enter through the delivery bay and are carried inward; salvage leaves a structure and is carried to storage. Both are carry-job flows over the same `Container` substrate.

## The pieces already exist as definitions nobody reads

Same pattern as the delivery bay in #96 — this is connecting declared content, not inventing it:

- `src/content/room-catalog.ts:143` — `room.storage-room`, `numericId: 15`, category `logistics`, requiring **2×** `object.storage-rack`.
- `src/content/object-catalog.ts:57` — `object.storage-rack`, capability `'item-storage'`.
- `src/simulation/operations/job.ts:54` — `submitCarryItem(input, createdAtTick)`, the carry substrate, already exercised end-to-end in `tests/unit/operations-representative-flows.test.ts`.

Neither room id nor object id is read by any simulation code today. They are part of the large set of catalog definitions with no consumer (11 of 18 room ids and 18 of 20 object ids, by a survey run in this session).

## What happens today instead

`ConstructionSystem.revertConstruction` (`src/simulation/construction/system.ts`) rewrites the tile's edge value and returns:

```ts
private revertConstruction(order: BuildOrder): void {
  const definition = getBuildableDefinition(order.definitionId);
  const edgeValue = edgeNumericIdFor(definition);
  if (edgeValue === 0) {
    this.markGeometryChanged(order.location);
    return;
  }
  const edge = resolveBuildEdge(order);
  this.writeEdge(order.location, edge, this.remainingEdgeValue(order, edge));
}
```

The wall is gone the instant the command runs. No time passes, nobody does the work, and nothing is produced. There is no salvage concept anywhere in the codebase.

## Direct consequence for PR #97 (open)

**This decision changes what #97 should do in one of its two cases, and #97 should be read as a placeholder there.**

#97 gives `ConstructionMaterialsProvider` a required `release(allocations)` and has `cancelOrder` call it, so cancellation returns materials to the container they were spent from. That is correct for one case and wrong for the other, and the two need separating:

| case | what happened physically | correct behaviour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| order cancelled **before it completed** (`materials-pending`, `assigned`, `in-progress`) | the materials were withdrawn but never became a structure | return them to the site container immediately — **what #97 does, and it is right** |
| order cancelled **after it completed** (`hadGeometry === true`) | a real wall existed and is now being taken apart | dismantle → salvage → **carry job to a storeroom**, which #97 does not do |

#91's own text flagged this gap before the decision existed:

> **Undo is a full refund with no waste.** Correct (undo means the build did not happen), but a future demolition/salvage model may want to revisit it.

This issue is that demolition/salvage model. #97 should still merge — instant return is strictly better than the current permanent destruction, and the completed-order case needs a storeroom, a salvage rate and a job, none of which exist yet. But the `hadGeometry` branch is now known to be temporary, and that should be recorded in the code rather than discovered again later.

Note also that #97's `release` deposits into the **same** container deliberately, to stay inside the no-teleport rule (`docs/OPERATIONS.md`). A dismantle that puts items in a storeroom on the other side of the prison **must** go through a carry job for exactly that reason — depositing directly into a remote storeroom would be the teleport the rule forbids.

## What this makes real

- **Storage capacity becomes a constraint.** Demolishing needs somewhere to put the output. A prison with no storeroom, or a full one, cannot absorb salvage.
- **Demolition costs work.** Someone has to take the thing apart and someone has to carry it. That competes with construction and with everything else the labour pool is doing.
- **Salvage is a supply source.** Under #96 materials are bought; salvage is the one route that produces materials without spending money. That makes demolition a genuine decision rather than an undo button.

## Open questions for the ADR

Recording these rather than deciding them:

- **Salvage rate.** Does dismantling recover 100% of what went in, or less? A full refund makes demolition free and rebuilding a no-op; total loss makes players never demolish. This is a balance decision and the two ends are both bad.
- **Is salvage the same item?** Does a dismantled brick wall yield `item.brick`, or a distinct lower-value `item.rubble`/`item.salvaged-brick`? A separate id lets salvage be worth less than new stock without inventing a pricing rule.
- **No storeroom, or a full one.** Is demolition refused, or does it proceed and strand the salvage on the floor? Refusing is legible; stranding needs a floor-stack concept that does not exist.
- **Does dismantling take time?** Today removal is instantaneous. A dismantle job with a duration is more honest but needs a reverse of the construction progress model.
- **Undo versus demolish.** Right now `undo()` and a player-initiated demolition are the *same* code path (`cancelOrder`). Under this decision they are different actions with different outcomes: undo means "I did not mean to do that", demolish means "take it apart and keep the parts". They probably need to stop being one function. This is the most structural of these questions.

## Scope

This issue is the decision and the ADR. The implementation depends on:

- #96 / #29 — money and procurement, so salvage has an economic meaning to sit against.
- A first consumer for `room.storage-room` and `object.storage-rack`, which nothing reads yet.
- #97 merging first, since it establishes the `release` seam this builds on.

Not in scope: salvage values, pricing, or a full demolition UI.

items.title: The room the game's own readout asks for next does not fit on the default screen: the yard needs 8×8, the reachable clear area is 12×11, and all a player gets is three different refusals
items.body:
Found by playing: `docs/research/2026-09-04-is-there-anything-to-do.md` **§0** (the clearance map), **§2.4** (three refused yards) and **§6.1** (the world is one chunk). Played on `origin/main` at v0.0.451 (`0e614c71`). Every code line below was re-opened on `origin/main` at v0.0.465 (`4c00eaba`).

This is the *next step* of the loop #938 established. #938 is that a room with no doorway is dead and every readout says it works. This is what happens to the player who fixes that: the roster then points them at the yard, and there is nowhere to put it.

## 1. The sequence, MEASURED (note §2.3, §2.4)

With one door per room the shower room works — `Hygiene` 98% / 100% / 96% at day +4 across three runs — and **the lowest-need column on the roster re-points itself onto `Recreation` and walks downward on its own**: 89 → 70 → 57 → 43 → 30% over four days in run A, replicated in B (74 → 31%) and C (76 → 33%). The note calls that column *"a working to-do list"*, and the room it is pointing at is the yard: `action.yard-recreation` is the only unblocked provider of `recreation` (`src/simulation/prisoners/actions.ts:165-167`).

**The yard could not be placed, three times, for three different reasons — and every refusal was correctly worded:**

| attempt | rectangle | what stopped it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| act 3, no pan | (19,13)–(26,20) | two corners land on the HUD: `div.save-panel__actions` and `button.ui-action hud-intake__admit`. **No command is submitted at all** |
| act 5 run B, 12 presses east | (26,10)–(33,17) | *"The room was not zoned — part of that area is outside the map."* Tiles 32 and 33 are past the single 32×32 chunk |
| act 5 run C, 6 presses east | (17,10)–(24,17) | *"The room was not zoned — it overlaps a room that is already there."* — eight times over eight retries |

## 2. The arithmetic, DERIVED over MEASURED facts

**MEASURED (note §0).** The clear-canvas map at 1440×900, probed tile by tile with `document.elementFromPoint`:

```
      5678901234567890123456
y= 9  ######################
y=10  ......................
y=11  ..................####
...
y=21  ######............####
y=22  ........######........
```

**The largest clear rectangle a player can build in without moving the camera is twelve tiles by eleven: x = 11..22, y = 11..21.** The starter 6×6 cell at (12,12)–(17,17) — the rectangle `buildAndPopulate` and every prior playtest uses — sits in the middle of it.

**VERIFIED, read.** `room.yard` requires `outdoors` and **8 × 8 / 64 tiles** (`src/content/room-catalog.ts:138-141`, exact). It asks for no walls, no objects and no money, so it is the cheapest room in the game.

**DERIVED.** Once a 6×6 cell sits at (12,12)–(17,17) and a 3×3 shower room at (19,15)–(21,17), **no 8×8 rectangle remains inside that 12×11** — every candidate crosses one of those rooms, runs into the HUD, or runs off the map at tile 31. So a player who builds a cell and then the room the game's own readout asks for has, on the default screen, nowhere left to put the room its readout asks for next.

## 3. The escapes exist and nothing points at them — VERIFIED, read

- **Panning works.** Twelve `ArrowRight` presses moved the world origin from (−304, −574) to (−1083, −574) — 779 px, about 12.2 tiles — and the clear rectangle after panning has the same 12 × 11 shape with the starter cell out of it. So the yard *is* placeable; what is not placeable is a yard **and** a 6×6 cell on one screen at 1440×900.
- **Zooming works** — `camera.zoom.out` is `Minus` (`src/input/bindings.ts:35`) — and **nothing on screen suggests it.** The note did not use it, and says why: every helper in its harness is built on `TILE = 64`, so measuring a zoomed run needs a calibration it does not have. **So "zooming out solves it" is untested here.**
- **There is no minimap to navigate with.** The panel is present in every dump and reads `Minimap is not available yet` (`src/content/default-locale-en.ts:391`) — which is #903 and #793.
- **The size requirement is stated, but late.** `NEEDS AT LEAST 8 × 8 TILES` appears only once `Yard` is the selected row in the Rooms list — after the player has already built the cell that takes the space.

## 4. The ceiling behind it, and one string that describes a state no command can change

**VERIFIED, read.** `createNewSimulationRuntime` builds `new SparseWorld(32)` (`src/simulation/runtime/new-session.ts:431`), loads chunk (0,0) and marks it owned at `:433`. `setOwned` has exactly three hits in `src/`: that call, the method itself (`src/simulation/world/sparse-world.ts:336`), and a comment in `src/simulation/prisoners/discharge-system.ts:77-78` that states the consequence in its own words — *"there is no gate: `world.setOwned` has one call site at session creation"*. There is no `BuyLand`, no `ClaimChunk` and no `ExpandPrison` among the fifteen declared commands (`src/simulation/protocol/commands.ts`, 15 `z.literal` command types).

**So every prison a player can start is tiles 0..31 on both axes.** That is 1,024 tiles, which at roughly six tiles per bed is a few hundred prisoners — **the cap is not what stops a player today**, and this issue does not file it as a defect. What it means is that the map is not a thing that grows, and the only expansion available is subdividing what is there.

**The small copy half, and it is checkable:** three shipped refusals tell the player they *do not own* land — `'The build order failed — you do not own that land.'` (`default-locale-en.ts:561`), `'The object was not placed — you do not own all of that land.'` (`:758`), `'The room was not zoned — you do not own all of that land.'` (`:812`) — while no command can make them own any. Ownership is set once, at session creation, and never again. **Note that these are not the refusals the note actually met:** past tile 31 the game answers `zone.out-of-bounds` (*"part of that area is outside the map"*), which is accurate. Whether `unowned-land` is reachable at all in a shipped prison is **not established here**, and is the first thing to check before touching those strings.

## 5. What a fix would be, and which part is the owner's

1. **Say how much room a room needs before the player spends the space** — the requirement text exists (`NEEDS AT LEAST 8 × 8 TILES`); what is missing is reaching a player who has not yet selected that row.
2. **Point at the camera.** Nothing in the interface suggests panning or zooming, and #794 already records that a player can pan into solid black with nothing telling them the way back. A yard that does not fit is the case where the camera is the answer and is never named.
3. **Reconsider the yard's 8×8** against the space a default screen actually offers, or against the starter camera's placement. **That is balance and catalogue tuning, and therefore the owner's** — an agent should not retune a room requirement to make a viewport work.
4. **Do not fix this by shrinking the HUD**; #899 and #517 are the viewport-pressure issues and this one is about the world, not the chrome.

## 6. The test that should have caught it, and the mutation

Nothing asserts that the rooms the catalogue offers can be placed in the space a fresh prison gives a player. The gate is cheap and does not need a browser: for each room type's `minimum-size`, assert a rectangle of that size exists inside the starting camera's clear area at the reference viewport — the clearance map in note §0 is the measurement it would encode. **The surviving mutation to state when this lands:** raise a room's `minWidth` past the clear area and watch it go red.

## 7. Weakest claim, and what would refute it

**The measured half is the geometry; the soft half is "nowhere left to put it".** The clearance map, the three refusals and the pan delta are all measurements at 1440×900. What is *not* established is that a player is stuck: **zooming out was never played** (note §14 states this outright — *"No yard was ever opened"*), and a player who pans first and builds the yard before the cell has the space. So the honest claim is: **on the default screen, in the order the game's own readouts ask for the rooms, the second room does not fit** — not that the yard is unreachable.

**What would refute it:** a run that zooms out with a recalibrated tile transform and places an 8×8 yard beside the starter cell, or a measurement at a viewport where the clear rectangle is 16 wide.

**Two instrument caveats the note reports about itself, carried forward:** the note made *three* geometry mistakes about this same 8×8 square (into the save panel, into the minimap, off the map) before it clamped the search to the world, and its screen dumps are **upper bounds** because `innerText` ignores a scroll container's clipping. The refusals and the `elementFromPoint` probes are measurements, not upper bounds.

Refs #938, #903, #793, #794, #899, #517, #886. Source: `docs/research/2026-09-04-is-there-anything-to-do.md` §0, §2.4, §6.1, §14.

items.title: [Prisoners] Cell allocation asks only about capacity, never about who is already in the room
items.body:
## Context

`RoomInstanceRegistry.assign(instanceId, entityId)` places a prisoner in a room if there is capacity. Capacity is the only question it asks. Who is already in there is not consulted.

Meanwhile the simulation already models gangs (`src/simulation/incidents/gangs.ts`), sector risk, and incidents with participants — so it already knows enough to say that two particular people should not share a cell, and never asks.

## What real practice does

England and Wales run a **Cell Sharing Risk Assessment**: before anyone is physically located in a shared cell, a rating is produced and must be recorded in the prison management system. Reception also includes health and mental-health screening by a qualified professional, and new arrivals typically spend their first night on a dedicated **first-night or induction wing** where staff watch them more closely, precisely because that is when risk is highest and least understood.

Sources: [HMPPS early days in custody](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/67488818ebabe47136b3a188/2024_11_04_PSI_07_2015_Early_Dates_in_Custody.pdf), [prison reception](https://prisonguide.co.uk/prison-reception-arrival-at-the-prison/), [intake assessment](https://www.ojp.gov/ncjrs/virtual-library/abstracts/prisoner-intake-systems-assessing-needs-and-classifying-prisoners).

## Why this is the highest-value single mechanic on the list

It is an **emergent-story generator built out of systems that already exist**. Cell allocation stops being a capacity puzzle and becomes a judgement with consequences that arrive later and elsewhere — which is exactly the property that separates a management sim worth replaying from a spreadsheet with sprites.

It also gives the player a reason to care about individuals rather than a population count. #75 just gave prisoners names; this is what makes a name mean something.

And unlike most gameplay proposals, it needs almost no new state: gang membership, incident history and classification are already modelled.

## Scope

- [ ] A compatibility check consulted at placement: gang affiliation, classification distance, shared incident history, vulnerability.
- [ ] A **rating**, not a boolean — some pairings are unwise rather than forbidden, and the interesting decisions live in the middle.
- [ ] The player can see *why* a pairing is flagged. An opaque refusal is not a mechanic, it is an error message.
- [ ] Overriding is possible and consequential. A game that simply forbids the risky choice has removed the decision.
- [ ] Bad pairings raise incident probability through the existing trigger system rather than a bespoke path.
- [ ] Determinism: same seed, same command stream, same outcomes.

## Related, and worth deciding together

`room.holding-cell` and `room.solitary-cell` already exist in the catalog, but there is **no first-night or induction accommodation** and no notion of a person being new. `IntakeSystem` has a `reception` stage that is a moment rather than a place. Real reception is a 30–45 day process with staged assessment; Lockstate's is instantaneous. Whether to model that as a phase is a design decision — but it is the natural home for this assessment, so decide it here rather than twice.

## Dependencies

- `src/simulation/prisoners/room-instance-registry.ts`, `intake-system.ts`
- `src/simulation/incidents/gangs.ts`, `trigger-system.ts`
- #78 (classification tiers) — the distance metric needs a scale to measure on
- #39 (traits and relationships) overlaps; sequence them so this does not get built twice

items.title: [Owner decisions] Eight calls taken 2026-08-29 — the player-facing queue is cleared
items.body:
The owner took eight decisions in one sitting on 2026-08-29, clearing the backlog that `AGENTS.md`'s fourth exclusion had been holding. Recorded here because they were taken in a chat session, and a chat session is ephemeral — this issue is the durable record, and the linked issues each carry the same call.

In every case the owner chose the **most thorough** option offered, consistent with the standing mandate's "quality over cheapness; cost is not a constraint".

---

## 1. #507 — build the event channel

**Decision: build one shared event channel.** `HudSeverity`'s `'info'` finally gets producers: sentence end, admission, sanction, insolvency warning.

Rejected: a status-strip readout only (covers the economy half, leaves the silent sentence-end), and case-by-case handling (which is how #508 and #509 were closed, and would have been the third time in a row while `'info'` stayed dead).

This unblocks #503 and half of #533. Every measured finding of 2026-08-29 falls into this one category: the prison computes what happens to it and renders none of it.

## 2. #529 — show every missing item, with quantities, and before zoning

**Decision: full list plus the catalogue row.** The panel lists every missing object with its quantity (`2 × Dining Table`), **and** the catalogue row shows requirements *before* the player zones, so a purchase can be planned.

Rejected: listing all missing items but leaving the pre-zoning catalogue untouched, and the minimal "keep one item, add a count".

The projection has known the quantities since #530 landed, so the data is already there. **This needs new player-facing copy with a numeral, and the owner authorised it knowing that** — the drafted strings should still be flagged for review in the PR that adds them.

## 3. #532 — give the kitchen an action, weaken the yard

**Decision: both halves.** The kitchen gets an action (cooking, feeding the canteen), and the yard gets a cost or a weaker score so the common room has a state in which it wins.

Rejected: leaving the yard strong and giving the common room a niche it alone serves, and hiding both rooms until they have a use.

Measured: zero common-room uses across an entire 18-day run, against 22 yard uses; and the kitchen has no entry in `DEFAULT_ACTIONS` at all.

## 4. #533 — add dismissal *and* stop demanding a guard at zero population

**Decision: both.** A dismiss command in the protocol and a control in the panel, **and** the coverage requirement stops asking for a guard when there is nobody to guard.

Rejected: either one alone. They are two different defects — one gives the player a way out of the trap, the other stops them walking into it by being obedient.

## 5. Sentence length — vary it

**Decision: sentences are drawn from a range at admission, with some clearly longer than 13,600 ticks.**

Rejected: a single longer constant, a player-chosen sentence at admission, and leaving 10,000 as it is.

Every admission from the HUD currently gets a hard-coded 10,000 ticks — 4.17 days, measured as exactly four payments then discharge in two independent runs. This is *why* the grant-withholding schedule is nearly unreachable: the two room-gated needs take 10,200 and 13,600 ticks to fall to the threshold, both longer than the sentence. Varying it activates a mechanic that already exists in the code and currently has no way to fire.

## 6. Need visibility — a bar per prisoner

**Decision: each prisoner in the roster shows their worst need as a bar.**

Rejected: a warning only at the withholding threshold (shows the fait accompli, not the trend), and a single prison-wide count (fits a phone, but names neither the prisoner nor the need).

The data already arrives — the roster projection carries `lowestNeed` and `src/ui/hud/regime-panel.ts:50` deliberately does not render it. This also removes a real measurement blocker: "the need was served" and "the need decayed but not far enough" are currently indistinguishable from outside the simulation, which blocked two measurements on 2026-08-29.

## 7. #517 — the Build panel collapses when the tool is armed

**Decision: arming a world tool collapses the panel to a bar, revealing the map; it returns after placement or on Escape.**

Rejected: rewording the hint to point at the coordinate form on narrow screens (honest, but leaves the phone without the gesture permanently), and a translucent panel (touch through a translucent layer is easy to get wrong in a way worse than the bug).

The owner plays on a phone, so this is a first-hand blocker rather than a theoretical one.

## 8. ADR 0051, 0052, 0054 — accept all three

**Decision: accept, with a review pass first.** All three read `Proposed, 2026-08-28. Not self-approved.` while the code they describe is live and unchallenged.

The owner's instruction was explicit: accept them, **but report back rather than quietly approving any ADR that describes something the code does not actually do.** A status is supposed to describe reality; that cuts both ways.

- `0051` — what a player sees for an order given while the clock is paused
- `0052` — drawing the world with the source art sheets
- `0054` — what a prisoner's day is made of when the prison is empty

Note for whoever does this: the STATUS-QUEUE anchor contract counts `Proposed` entries (22 at last anchor), so this pass moves that tally and the next re-anchor must read it fresh.

---

## What is still the owner's

This clears the queue that existed on 2026-08-29. It does not change the standing exclusions: a server-side execution surface, `supabase/migrations/`, deploy configuration, and any *new* player-visible promise the code does not keep.

items.title: [Roadmap] Execute Lockstate implementation backlog
items.body:
> **Corrected — 2026-08-24.** Re-verified against `main` at `9b6965a` (v0.0.16).
>
> **Two documentation paths cited by this issue have never existed in any commit on any branch.** Verified independently:
> ```
> $ git log --all --oneline --diff-filter=A --name-only -- 'docs/specs/**' 'docs/research/NEW_FEATURES.md'
> (empty)
> $ git ls-tree --name-only origin/main docs/research/
> docs/research/ARCHITECTURE_PATTERN_AUDIT.md
> ```
> Every reference to `docs/specs/` and to `docs/research/NEW_FEATURES.md` is removed below. The sentences around them are rewritten rather than left dangling.
>
> **One checked Definition-of-Done box asserted a state that never held** and is deleted: *"- [x] Imported specifications and product research are available under `docs/` on `main`."* Nothing was ever imported under those paths, so that box could not have been true when it was ticked. Its sibling, *"Imported specification areas are represented by actionable issues"*, is kept — the issues exist and are the thing that actually carried the plan.
>
> **Eight dependency boxes were unticked while their subject had shipped**, all of them for issues that are now closed. Re-ticked against the tree, with the directory that implements each named beside it. #20 is deliberately **left unticked**: its SQL has been executed since (see #20), but nothing in `src/` can reach Supabase, so the issue is genuinely open.
>
> Nothing else is changed. `tests/foundation/documentation-links-contract.test.ts` passes on all of this because it only checks links *inside* `docs/`, never issue bodies — no gate in this repository can see a dead path cited from a tracker.

## Context

Lockstate now has its production-oriented foundation on `main`: reproducible tooling, strict TypeScript, Cloudflare Workers Static Assets delivery, testing and benchmark contracts, and the versioned simulation-worker protocol.

Concrete data shapes, algorithms and subsystem boundaries for ROADMAP Phases 1–11 are carried by the individual issues below and by the ADRs they cite. Those are planning input, not a replacement for `AGENTS.md`, `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`, accepted ADRs or issue-level review.

## Goal

4. Executable GitHub Issues.

items.title: [Economy] Implement auditable ledger, grants, recurring costs and prison labor income
items.body:
> **Correction — 2026-08-24.** The Dependencies list ended with a line containing only a full stop — the remains of a sentence that cited a `docs/specs/` path. **`docs/specs/` has never existed in any commit on any branch** (`git log --all --oneline --diff-filter=A --name-only -- 'docs/specs/**'` returns nothing), so there is nothing to restore and the stray character is removed. **Nothing else is changed**; the substance was re-checked against `main` at `9b6965a` (v0.0.16) and is accurate. Note for readers arriving from the roadmap: a first slice of this issue shipped in #249/#250 as `src/simulation/economy/` (a `Treasury` and a `ProcurementSystem`); the ledger, grants, recurring costs and labour income below are all still open.

## Context
A single mutable cash balance cannot explain why money changed, support reports or debug save/replay discrepancies. Economy must be an integer-minor-unit ledger driven by typed transactions from construction, staffing, procurement, grants and production.

## Goal
Create the deterministic financial foundation and a representative operating loop without committing final balance values.

## In scope
- Integer minor-unit money type and overflow/validation rules.
- Append-only typed ledger entries with source, category, amount, tick/time, related entity/order and description key.
- Derived balance and period summaries from ledger state.
- Initial capital/grant records and grant objective/progress hooks.
- Recurring wages, utilities, maintenance and food/procurement charges.
- Construction purchase/commit/refund integration.
- Representative workshop/prison-labor production and sale transaction hooks using real inventories/jobs.
- Budget/forecast/report projections and shortage/insolvency policy hooks.
- Versioned serialization/migrations and deterministic ordering.

## Out of scope
- Final pricing/balance and monetization.
- Real-world tax/accounting simulation.
- Unbounded floating-point currency.
- Full research/unlock/program systems owned by Issue #30.
- Direct UI mutation of balance.

## Dependencies
- Issue #16 construction orders/materials.
- Issue #23 definitions.
- Issue #25 jobs/inventories/utilities.
- Issue #18 save schema.

## Architecture notes
- Balance is a derived projection; every change has a ledger entry.
- Money uses integers; percentages/rates produce explicitly rounded entries.
- Recurring charges run through deterministic schedules and are idempotent per period.
- Workshop income requires completed production and inventory transfer, not passive arbitrary ticks.
- Grants/objectives emit/consume domain events rather than querying UI state.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] All representative money changes produce typed auditable entries.
- [ ] Derived balance equals ledger sum and survives save/replay.
- [ ] Duplicate scheduled charges for one period are prevented.
- [ ] Construction cancellation/refund follows explicit policy and ledger trace.
- [ ] Wages/utilities/food/maintenance integrate with real operational quantities.
- [ ] Workshop income requires completed jobs/items/sale transaction.
- [ ] Reports group entries by period/category/source without changing simulation state.
- [ ] Large/invalid amounts fail safely without floating-point drift.

## Test requirements
- Ledger invariants, sum and ordering tests.
- Recurring charge idempotency and rounding tests.
- Construction/procurement/refund integration tests.
- Workshop production/sale conservation tests.
- Save/migration/replay hash tests.

## Performance requirements
- Period reports should use maintained aggregates/indexing as history grows; avoid rescanning unlimited entries every frame.
- Benchmark representative multi-year ledger/report workloads.

## Documentation updates
- Money/rounding/ledger categories and transaction ownership.
- Initial grant and recurring-cost model.

## Definition of Done
- [ ] Every currency mutation is auditable and deterministic.
- [ ] Representative income/cost flows use real subsystems.
- [ ] Economy is serializable, reportable and ready for balance work.

items.title: OWNER RULINGS 2026-08-31: four of the five questions Part E put to the owner
items.body:
Four decisions taken by the owner on 2026-08-31, against the five yes/no questions in Part E of `docs/research/2026-08-31-playing-the-nine-changes.md`. Filed because they were taken in a chat session and a chat session is ephemeral — this issue is the durable record, in the same shape as #535 and #639.

Each was put with what the code does today, what it costs to leave alone, and a stated recommendation. **Two of the four went against the recommendation offered, and both are recorded as taken rather than as argued with.**

---

## 1. The escape sentence and the all-clear in one tick — **the alerts log opens by default**

**Ruling: the alerts list starts unfolded**, so both rows are readable without a click.

Rejected: suppressing the all-clear on a tick that recorded a successful escape (the recommendation offered), showing two rows in the band, and leaving it alone.

**What was measured.** `lapse` records the escape (`response-system.ts:620`) then `reportAllClearIfCalm` (`:625`) — same tick, consecutive sequences. The band keeps the newest event only (`simulation-events.ts:356`), and the alerts list that holds both starts folded (`hud-state.ts:53`) and caps at 8 rows (`MAX_EVENT_ALERT_ROWS`, `simulation-events.ts:265`, dropping the oldest). Result: the escape sentence is **written three times and painted zero times**. The player reads *"A prisoner is trying to break out."* for 7.6 s, then an all-clear saying the attempt was contained, and the log had dropped the row by the time it could be opened.

**Accepted cost, stated: a fixed slice of screen height at every width.** The strip is already the narrower half of this problem — 0 of 8 chips at 768px per #639's third ruling.

**What this ruling does not settle, and is put back to the owner below.** Two things survive it:

- **The 8-row cap.** A row pushed out by `MAX_EVENT_ALERT_ROWS` is still gone whether the list is folded or not, so an escape during a busy tick can still be unreadable.
- **The all-clear's wording after a successful escape.** It says the incident is over on a tick where a prisoner left; unfolding the list makes both sentences visible side by side, which makes the contradiction *more* legible rather than less. That is the fourth exclusion's own subject — a promise the code does not keep — so no wording is proposed here.

## 2. Money the game spends for the player — **out of the fold, with its Cancel**

**Ruling: the spent amount and the control that reverses it both come out of the *Buy* fold.**

Rejected: surfacing the amount alone and leaving the reversal behind a click; leaving both in the fold.

**What was measured.** `deliveriesBlock` is the last child of `buyRow` and `buyRow.hidden = true` (`build-panel.ts:1293-1311`); the row and its `Cancel` measure 0×0. #640 removed the need to open the fold at all, and #693 fixed a refund whose only trigger lives inside it.

Consistent with the standing directive — *"gra ma być łatwa przyjazna do grania, a nie jakieś ukryte funkcje"*. A charge the player did not order, and the way to undo it, are the two least hideable things in the panel.

## 3. Discovered contraband — **name the item**

**Ruling: the message names what was found**, using the five `contraband.*.name` keys already authored.

Rejected: naming the weapon alone; leaving the bare count.

**What was measured.** The strip shows `itemsDiscovered` as a bare count (`status-strip-projection.ts:552`). All five name keys are authored and unused — `grep -rn "contraband\.weapon\.name" src/ui/` returns nothing. After #681 a weapon is reachable, so a found phone and a found weapon render as the same character.

**No new player-facing copy is needed**: the strings exist and lack only a reader. Any string that turns out to be missing is proposed for sign-off rather than invented.

## 4. High risk on screen — **a strip chip and a roster sorted by tier**

**Ruling: both.** `prisonersHighRisk` reaches the screen, and the Regime roster sorts by tier instead of by arrival order.

Rejected: sorting alone; the chip alone; leaving it.

**What was measured.** The count crosses the protocol and no strip item reads it. `PRISONER_ROSTER_ROW_LIMIT = 4` (`regime-panel.ts:156`) and the projection pages by entity index with no sort. After #681 the tier is the gate on a weapon **and** on an escape, and the player's view of it is four rows in arrival order.

Both read data already crossing the protocol. The row limit itself is not raised by this ruling — four rows showing the four highest tiers is the whole of what was asked for.

---

## Still outstanding after this issue

- **Part E item 5** — should the refusal band have a lifetime, or a removal refusal a coarser key? The counts payload carries `RefusalLog.last` for ever (`state-machine.ts:559`) and a removal's supersession key is the tile (`refusal-log.ts:538`), so one misclick with *Remove* armed leaves a red sentence up for the rest of the session.
- **Two smaller wording items**, both from Part E's foot: the duplicate-order sentence names an *order* where the player sees a *wall* (§1d), and a refused *Admit* the main thread diagnosed itself is reported without the cause it diagnosed, while the sentence for that cause ships in the same file (§12a).
- **The two residues of ruling 1** named under it: the 8-row cap, and what the all-clear should say on a tick that recorded a successful escape.
- **ADRs 0052 and 0054**, whose acceptance #535 decision 8 made conditional on a review pass reported to the owner. Neither has had one. (ADR 0051 was accepted by #639 and recorded by #647; the count and the handover were corrected by #702.)

## What is still the owner's

Unchanged: a server-side execution surface, `supabase/migrations/`, deploy configuration, and any *new* player-visible promise the code does not keep.

items.title: [Measured] The tick-cost case for pruning dormant systems is false; navigation is the real cost; and removing a save section costs a V5 bump
items.body:
Five game-design researchers were independently asked what to prune from this codebase, given that eleven of thirteen registered systems iterate permanently empty collections. All five recommended cutting or deferring the utility network, contraband, incidents and the container/job-board/worker-pool trio. **None of them measured anything** — they had no repository access. Three of them asserted mutually exclusive costs, so at most one could be right.

This issue records the measurements, because two of their conclusions are wrong in ways that would cost real work if acted on, and one is right for a reason nobody stated.

Method: throwaway harness outside the repo driving the real `createNewSimulationRuntime`, three independent interleaved runs of 21 rounds × 200,000 `Kernel.step()` calls per configuration, round-robined so drift hits every configuration equally. Node 24 under vitest, not a browser worker — `docs/BENCHMARKING.md` forbids timing assertions for that reason, and the third digit below is noise. `benchmarks/harness.mjs` could not be reused directly: its `kernel-throughput` scenario is a synthetic re-implementation of the kernel in plain JS and says so in its own comment.

## The per-tick cost, measured

| Configuration | ns/tick (median of 3 runs) |
|---|---|
| bare `Kernel`, 0 systems — the loop floor | 18.0 / 18.7 / 18.7 |
| navigation only | 423.2 / 435.5 / 438.7 |
| the 12 empty-iterating systems, no navigation | 276.5 / 282.8 / 282.9 |
| **all 13, as shipped** | **736.3 / 772.0 / 791.5** |

**The twelve empty-iterating systems cost 260–350 ns/tick together.** At the real clock rate (`FixedStepClock.stepMilliseconds = 50`, so 20 ticks/s at ×1 and 80 at ×4) that is **0.0007 % of one second at ×1 and 0.003 % at ×4**. Even at the tick loop's own ceiling of 5 ticks per 15 ms wake — 333 ticks/s — it is 0.01 %.

**Navigation alone costs 405–420 ns/tick above the floor — more than all twelve empty systems combined, and 55 % of a shipped tick.** It is the audit's third category: it runs and does real work nothing reads. The cost is `ensureGraph()`'s `.map()` + `.filter()` allocation and an `isNavigationGraphStale` scan **every tick** (`src/simulation/navigation/navigation-system.ts:108-116,121`).

So: if per-tick cost is ever the reason to change something here, **the target is navigation's per-tick graph check, not the empty iterators.** The empty iterators are noise; the system doing real work nobody reads is the expensive one.

The mechanism the researchers guessed at is real, for the record — `EntityQuery.execute()` allocates one empty array per call (`src/simulation/entity/query.ts:37-47`), `IncidentTriggerSystem.update` allocates and sorts a copy of an empty array (`trigger-system.ts:63`), `SearchSystem.update` calls `activeJobsInCanonicalOrder()` (`search-system.ts:142`). The mechanism is just four orders of magnitude short of mattering against a frame budget.

## The claim about the worker boundary is wrong in every particular

One researcher asserted that keeping utility state *"triples the spatial grid data transferred across the Web Worker boundary per tick."*

1. **Nothing carrying utility state crosses per tick.** The tick loop (`src/simulation/worker/state-machine.ts:200-217`) posts exactly two things, both rate-limited: `simulation/clock-state` at most every 250 ms (**47 B**) and `simulation/status-counts` at most every 500 ms (**206 B**, eleven integers, additionally skipped when no count changed). Asserted: `/utilit|electric|water/i` against the counts payload is `false`. The full session bundle crosses only on `simulation/request-snapshot`, which the render feed sends at most every 2 s.
2. **Utility is not in the spatial-grid section.** It lives in `payload.simulation.operations`; the grid is `payload.world`. Removing it cannot change `bundle.world` by one byte.
3. **The magnitude is inverted.** Fresh session, JSON bytes: whole bundle **2,998 B**, `bundle.world` **243 B**, `operations.electricity` **69 B** + `operations.water` **63 B** = **132 B**, i.e. **4.40 % of the snapshot**. Even summing it wrongly into the grid gives ×1.54, not ×3. After 5,000 ticks all three figures are unchanged, because nothing writes it.

## The trio should be kept, and the researchers' framing was inverted

All five treated the container/job-board/worker-pool trio as unregistered speculative infrastructure, and one argued explicitly that "built and not even registered" is a weaker category than "runs every tick but empty", so the trio is likelier to be incomplete.

**`JobSystem` is registered** — `src/simulation/runtime/new-session.ts:353`, id `operations.jobs`, order 260, `intervalTicks: 5`. It is in the shipped `systemExecutionOrder` and in the pinned list at `tests/determinism/kernel-system-order.test.ts:175`. **Construction consumes the container substrate for real**: `ConstructionSystem` is wired to a `ContainerMaterialsProvider` over a `Container` (`new-session.ts:210-213`), which is also `ProcurementSystem`'s deposit target (`:227`).

And the "more speculative" hypothesis is refuted by test evidence pointing the other way. Four of the eight `operations-*` test files drive the trio **through a real `Kernel` with `kernel.step()`**, not by poking methods — including `tests/unit/operations-scale.test.ts`, which runs **300 carry jobs across 20 workers for 3,000 kernel ticks and asserts all 300 complete with 300 bricks in the destination container**. By contrast the utility tests are direct-method only and *cannot* be otherwise, because `UtilityNetwork` has no `update()` to schedule. That is the real distinction between the two items, and it separates them in the opposite direction from the claim.

This is complete, kernel-verified machinery at scale waiting on a job producer — the same shape as `PurchaseMaterials` and `ZoneRoom`. Deleting it would delete the only working logistics loop in the repository, to save 16–18 ns/tick.

## The utility network is the one clean cut, for a different reason

Not registered and cannot be: `UtilityNetwork` declares no `id`, `order`, `schedule` or `update()`, so it does not satisfy `SystemRegistration`. Both instances are constructed (`new-session.ts:237-238`) and exposed on the runtime (`:377-378`); the registration block is `:349-359` and neither appears. `evaluate()` — the whole reason the class exists — has **20 call sites, every one in a test file, none in `src/`**. No projection mentions it.

So its per-tick cost is not small, it is **zero** — it never runs. The case for cutting is dead weight, not performance: 183 LOC, 12 tests, 132 B of save schema that cannot change, and three enum groups in `src/content/simulation-message-keys.ts:449-465` whose `sourceFile` points at the module.

One thing worth deciding rather than assuming: `src/ui/save-panel.ts:101` renders `save.scope.operations` = *"jobs, containers and utility networks"* after a restore. The utility section genuinely is snapshotted and restored, so the string is not false — but it advertises to the player a capability that can only ever be empty. Whether that is worth rewording is a product call, not a defect I should quietly fix.

## Removing anything from the save costs a V5 bump — this is the load-bearing constraint

`operationsSectionSchema` (`src/persistence/save-schema.ts:424-436`) is a **single shared object**, referenced once from `sessionSystemsSchemaFor` (`:784-795`), which both V3 and V4 instantiate (`:797,799`). Every object is `.strict()`, and `docs/PERSISTENCE.md` states the consequence: an undeclared key is not trimmed, it fails the whole save.

**So deleting `electricity`/`water` from that object rejects every V3 and V4 save on disk as `invalid-shape`.** A removal costs three coordinated edits: freeze a historical copy of the schema that still declares the keys and point V3/V4 at it (the "never edited once registered" convention the migration chain already follows at `:964-968`); bump `SAVE_SCHEMA_VERSION` to 5; register a V4→V5 step that strips them.

That is more work than 132 B is worth on its own — which is the argument for **unregistering and ceasing to encode** the deferred subsystems now, and doing **one combined V5 bump later** that drops every dead section at once, rather than four separate bumps.

For scale on what such a bump would reclaim: `payload.simulation` is **1,863 B of a 2,998 B bundle (62.1 %)** across 32 second-level fields, and **30 of those 32 exist only for machinery nothing in the app can reach.** The two exceptions carry values that also cannot change from the app — `operations.containers` is always `[["construction-materials",[]]]` because `PurchaseMaterials` has no producer, and `economy.treasury` is permanently the opening balance for the same reason. `navigation.doors` is `{"doors":[]}` for ever, because nothing in `src/` calls `DoorRegistry.register` outside the restore codec.

## Gate cost, exact

Unregistering costs **one edit**: the 13-entry `{id, order}` list at `tests/determinism/kernel-system-order.test.ts:167-183`. The distinctness and ascending-order assertions at `:185-192` still hold after a deletion.

Two cascades are worth knowing before anyone starts:

- **Cutting contraband forces an eleven→ten cascade across three files.** `tests/foundation/documentation-claims-contract.test.ts:230-274` counts the `readonly \w+: number;` fields in `status-strip-projection.ts`'s `counts` block, maps the count through a number-word table, and requires that word to appear as "*N* integers" in `docs/HUD_PROJECTIONS.md`, `docs/adr/0003-simulation-worker-protocol.md` **and** `src/simulation/worker/state-machine.ts`. Removing `contrabandDiscovered` makes all three false in the same change. The gate's own docblock records this class of drift having happened once already.
- **Deleting the utility module fails a message-key gate** unless the same change removes all three enum groups whose `sourceFile` names it: `tests/unit/simulation-message-keys.test.ts:178` asserts the file exists, `:189` requires each group's declaration to be found inside it.
- `tests/foundation/unconsumed-content-contract.test.ts:198-204` asserts `{declared: 62, unconsumedBySrcAndTests: 34, unconsumedBySrcOnly: 53}` exactly, in both directions, deliberately. Deleting the contraband *catalog* (5 ids, all referenced only from `tests/`) takes it to `{57, 29, 48}`; deleting the contraband *systems* while keeping the catalog changes it not at all, since all five ids already have zero `src/` references.

## Recommendation

- **Utility network — cut**, accepting that the save-schema half waits for a combined V5 bump.
- **Container / job-board / worker-pool — keep.** It is registered, kernel-verified at 300-job scale, and consumed by construction.
- **Contraband, incidents — unregister and stop encoding; keep the code and its tests.** Both are two orders of magnitude below mattering per tick (~6 ns and ~4.5 ns respectively); the reason is that they occupy kernel slots and 14 save fields while sitting three unreachable entry points away from doing anything. `docs/CONTRABAND.md`'s withheld-ground-truth design is a real asset and `contraband-projection.ts` already implements it.
- **Do not cut anything for tick cost.** If that ever becomes the reason, measure navigation first.

Two incident types can never occur, for the record: `IncidentType` declares `assault | escape-attempt | riot | gang-retaliation` (`incident.ts:6`) and the only openers are `openRiot` and `tryOpenRetaliation`. `assault` and `escape-attempt` have no producer in `src/` at all.

## Not measured

Structured-clone wire size (JSON bytes used as the proxy — section *ratios* are sound, absolutes are JSON, which is also what the persistence layer writes). Browser worker tick cost. Attribution of the twelve to better than ±50 ns, because registering twelve more `update` implementations makes the kernel call site polymorphic and changes how navigation itself is compiled — the two routes disagree by 55–90 ns and both are reported. Cost with non-empty collections, which is a different question; `tests/perf/fixtures/prison-fixture.ts` exists for it.

## Related

- #261 — the reachability audit these systems come from.
- #287 — two more producers missing (`GuardRoster.hire`, `SessionController.importInto`).
- #285 — the treasury has no reachable credit path.

items.title: [Rooms] A mis-zoned cell that acquires an occupant can never be un-zoned, and no command moves a prisoner out of accommodation
items.body:
## The trap

Found while verifying #337 (PR #475), and flagged there as out of that issue's scope.

Un-zoning a room whose instance still has a claim is **refused**: `unzone.room-occupied` at `src/simulation/rooms/zoning.ts:753`, surfaced to the player as *"Nothing was removed — somebody is using that room."* That refusal is correct as a refusal — the alternative is dropping a room out from under the prisoner living in it, and `RoomInstanceRegistry.unregister` throws a `RangeError` rather than allow it (`src/simulation/prisoners/room-instance-registry.ts:257`, now guarded by PR #475).

The problem is the **exit**. A search found no command that moves a prisoner out of accommodation. So the sequence is:

1. The player zones a cell somewhere they later regret — the wrong corner, the wrong shape, in the way of a corridor they now want.
2. Time passes. The cell gets a bed. An admission assigns a prisoner to it.
3. The player tries to un-zone it. Refused, correctly, and permanently.
4. There is no way to empty the cell. The only exit is that prisoner's sentence ending.

The room is now a fixture of the prison for the rest of that prisoner's sentence, and the player has no move. Nothing in the refusal message says that, either: *"somebody is using that room"* reads as "try again later", and later never arrives by any action the player can take.

## Why this is not #337

#337 was the un-zone command taking too much — adjacency-plus-type standing in for room identity, fixed at `dea529c`. This is the opposite end: the command taking nothing, for ever, with no route to change that. #337's verification pass confirmed the refusal is a *defined* outcome; it did not establish that it is the *right* one, and the agent named that as its weakest claim.

## Why it is not a correctness bug

Every piece behaves as designed. This is a **playability** defect: a state a player can enter by an ordinary mistake and cannot leave. That is the shape #411 was — "not an awkward game, an unfinishable one" — one notch less severe, because the prison keeps running.

## In scope

Deciding what a player may do about an occupied room they no longer want. Candidates, not a menu to pick from without research:

- **A reassignment command** — move a prisoner to another suitable accommodation, refusing when none is free. This is the honest one, and it is also the one that needs the most thought: it touches the accommodation assignment path, ADR 0029's claim model, and probably ADR 0041.
- **A deferred un-zone** — the designation is marked for removal and takes effect when the last claim clears. Cheap, but it introduces a pending state the save format and the HUD both have to carry, and a player who forgets they queued it gets a room vanishing later for no visible reason.
- **A better refusal** — leave the mechanic and make the message say *why* and *until when*. Not a fix, but it converts an invisible trap into a stated rule, and it is the right thing to do regardless of which of the above is chosen.

Any of these is a player-visible promise, so if the chosen answer cannot be kept by the code, that half is the owner's.

## Out of scope

- Changing the refusal into a silent success. Dropping a room from under its occupant is the failure `RoomInstanceRegistry.unregister` exists to prevent.
- The **traveller** case — a room un-zoned out from under a prisoner in transit, who holds no claim (ADR 0029). That is already handled by ADR 0041 and pinned by `tests/integration/unzoned-target-mid-journey.test.ts`.
- The V4-save residual recorded in PR #475 (two rectangle-less instances still both clear on one drag). Different mechanism, deliberately left.

## Required verification

Reproduce the trap end to end before designing: zone a cell, let it be furnished and occupied, attempt the un-zone, and show there is no sequence of available commands that frees it. Then show the chosen answer frees it — and show that the case it must **still** refuse is still refused.

**A green suite is not a guarded suite.** Mutate the new behaviour away by hand, watch red, restore by hand, watch green, both outputs in the commit message. Note that the refusal path is reachable from `pnpm test`; if the answer adds a control, that control is unreachable there — `vitest.config.ts` runs `environment: 'node'` with no jsdom — and needs a `tests/browser/` spec.

## Dependencies

`src/simulation/rooms/zoning.ts`, `src/simulation/prisoners/room-instance-registry.ts`, ADR 0022, ADR 0029, ADR 0041. Related: #337 (closed by PR #475), #434 (contention fairness in the same allocation path).

items.title: [Hygiene] Unreachable code and unconsumed content are the majority case, not the exception — inventory, and what should happen to each
items.body:
Split from **#124 items 9 and 10**, filed as one issue because the two overlap heavily (the barrel files appear in both) and because the *decision* is the same one each time: is this waiting for a consumer, or is it finished with?

**This issue asks for owner judgement more than it proposes work.** #124's own instruction applies: *"Err toward 'needs owner judgement' — recommending deletion of something load-bearing is far worse than leaving something inert."* Nothing here should be deleted on an agent's initiative.

---

## ⛔ Read this first: three catalog entries must NOT be removed

`room.delivery-bay`, `object.loading-dock-door` and `room.storage-room` are in the unconsumed set below **and are load-bearing for planned work.** ADR 0017 (merged, `Proposed`) names all three as the intended physical route for material procurement, and #99 makes the storeroom the destination for salvage. Deleting them as dead content would remove the thing two decisions depend on.

They are the clearest illustration of why this issue is a judgement call: *"has no consumer"* and *"is dead"* are not the same statement.

---

## The inventory, as measured

### Subsystems reachable only from their own tests

| area | lines | reachable from `src/main.ts`? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `src/simulation/presentation/` | 2,349 | no — **already filed as #104, do not re-file** |
| `src/services/telemetry/` | 763 | no |
| `src/services/entitlements/` | 883 | no |
| `src/services/challenges/` | 552 | no |
| `src/persistence/cloud/` | 324 | no |

`src/main.ts` touches `src/services/` exactly twice, both times from `services/localization/`.

That is roughly **4,871 lines** of specified, tested, unreachable code. **This is not automatically a problem** — ADR 0008 defines the trusted-service boundary as a contract to build against, and #121's doc sweep has just corrected `ARCHITECTURE.md` to stop describing the cloud path as something the app reaches. Specified-ahead-of-use is a legitimate state. What is missing is anywhere that *says* which of these is awaiting a consumer and which is speculative.

**#104 is the one with a decision already attached** — four independent analyses ranked the projection channel highest value-per-effort, precisely because those 2,349 lines become reachable the moment the channel exists.

### Content declared and never read

| catalog | declared | referenced by no code |
| --- | --- | --- |
| room ids | 18 | **11** |
| object ids | 20 | **18** |
| staff-role ids | 8 | **5** |
| derived simulation-enum locale keys | 166 | **164** |

The assembled `en` catalog holds ~259 keys; production looks up **54** (the 52 in `HUD_MESSAGE_KEY` plus two build-edge keys derived in `build-panel.ts`).

**This is the fact most worth internalising from #124**, and it generalises: *never assume a catalog entry has a consumer.* It is why the `'brick'` / `'item.brick'` split (fixed in #97) went unnoticed — two vocabularies that had never met, because nothing had ever supplied a material through the catalog.

### Barrel files with no importer

`src/persistence/local/index.ts`, `src/persistence/cloud/index.ts`, `src/persistence/session/index.ts`, `src/rendering/build/index.ts`, `src/simulation/worker/index.ts`, `src/ui/primitives/index.ts`, plus `src/persistence/index.ts` and `src/services/index.ts` which are referenced only from prose.

⚠️ **`src/persistence/cloud/index.ts` is the *only* path by which `supabase-client.ts` is reachable** — removing that barrel orphans the client. Worth knowing before treating barrels as uniformly inert.

### Input subsystem

`src/input/pointer.ts`, `src/input/accessibility.ts`, and the settings-persistence API in `storage.ts`/`settings.ts`. The barrel makes the tree look reachable; production consumes three symbols. `PointerInputAdapter` is never constructed outside tests and the entire accessibility module is unused.

**Accessibility being unused is worth flagging as a product question, not a cleanup one.** AGENTS.md boundary 10 requires input to support remapping, QWERTY/AZERTY and touch — an unused accessibility module is either an unfinished commitment or a wrong one, and either answer is more interesting than deleting it.

### `tsconfig.json` lists a file that does not exist

`worker-configuration.d.ts` is included, does not exist, is generated by nothing, and is not gitignored. It is what `wrangler types` emits for a Worker's `Env` bindings — but `wrangler.jsonc` declares no `main`, so this assets-only Worker has no bindings to type.

**TypeScript silently ignores an absent listed file**, so `tsc -b` stays clean and the entry is invisible. This one is unambiguous: it should go, or something should generate it.

---

## Archive candidates, with the confidence the sweep assigned

### Certain — mechanical, no judgement needed

| path | why |
| --- | --- |
| `package.json` `smoke:deployment` | a strict subset of `verify:deployment`, which is the CI gate. **Two names invite running the weaker one and believing the gate ran** — that is the actual risk, not the duplication |
| `package.json` `build:production` | a pure alias of `build`, which already builds production; nothing references it |
| `tsconfig.json`'s `worker-configuration.d.ts` entry | see above |

### Needs owner judgement

| path | why |
| --- | --- |
| `public/game-content/source-art/` (23 PNGs) + `source-art.v1.json` | **24 files published to the deployed site and loaded by nothing.** No module in `src/` fetches the catalog or any image under it; the renderer's only asset path is `AtlasLibrary.load()` → `/assets/actors/asset-registry.json`. Duplicates bytes already in `assets/source/`. Note #140: the contract test over this catalog never actually hashes the images, so its integrity is unverified too |
| `tooling/build-source-art-catalog.mjs` | generates the above and is invoked by **nothing** — not `package.json`, not a workflow, not another script. Its only mention is prose in `docs/ART_PIPELINE.md`. **So editing an input silently does not regenerate the committed output**, which is the real defect here rather than the file's existence |
| `tooling/blender/create-environment-catalog.py` + `assets/source/blender/environment.mvp.catalog.blend` + `.manifest.json` | a closed loop with no exit: invoked by nothing, documented nowhere. `ART_PIPELINE.md` documents five sibling scripts and never mentions this one |
| `docs/research/ARCHITECTURE_PATTERN_AUDIT.md` | a 2026-08-22 audit whose questions have since been settled by accepted ADRs. Also names `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md` as the mechanism for recording adapted third-party code — **that file does not exist**, which is a live doc-truth defect regardless of what happens to the audit |
| `src/persistence/index.ts`, `src/services/index.ts` | barrels referenced only from prose |

---

## What would actually improve things, beyond deleting files

Deleting inert files is the least valuable outcome available here. Two changes would be worth more:

1. **Make "declared but unconsumed" a visible, checked state rather than a discovery.** A test or a generated report that lists catalog entries and locale keys with no consumer would turn a repeated four-agent sweep into a line of output — and would have caught the `'brick'`/`'item.brick'` split. It must support an explicit allowlist with reasons, because the delivery bay, the dock door and the storeroom are *supposed* to be in that list right now.
2. **Make the art catalog regenerate, or stop committing its output.** A generator nothing invokes, producing a committed artefact whose integrity test does not check its contents (#140), is the shape that silently goes stale.

## Deliberately not in this issue

- **#104** — the presentation layer. Filed, ranked, and has a decision attached.
- **Anything under `supabase/`** — the SQL is verified by 89 pgTAP assertions and is not dead.
- **`.gitignore` coverage of generated output** — folded into #138 with the other CI-hygiene items.

items.title: [Reachability] Two finished capabilities have no caller: hiring a guard, and importing a save
items.body:
Both are the same shape as #89 (`PurchaseMaterials`) and the `ZoneRoom` gap: a finished, tested capability with **no producer anywhere in `src/`**. Neither is recorded as an issue today. Both are measured below.

Filing them together because they share that shape, not because they share a surface — they want separate changes.

## 1. Nothing can hire a guard

```
$ git grep -n "\.hire(" origin/main -- src
(no output)

$ git grep -n "hire(" origin/main -- src
src/simulation/security/guard-roster.ts   # the definition, and nothing else
```

`GuardRoster.hire` is the only way a guard enters the roster. Ten modules under `src/simulation/` reference `GuardRoster` — `security/patrol-system.ts`, `security/deployment-system.ts`, `incidents/response-system.ts`, `contraband/search-system.ts`, `presentation/staff-projection.ts`, `identity/actor-identity.ts`, `runtime/new-session.ts`, `runtime/session-systems.ts` — and **not one of them calls `hire`**. So the roster is permanently empty, `allGuardIds()` returns nothing, and the patrol, deployment, incident-response and contraband-search systems iterate an empty collection for that reason specifically.

The consequence a player sees: the **Staff** readout is a real projection of real state and is permanently `0`.

This is not the same gap as the missing `ZoneRoom` producer. Zoning is blocked on a content decision about capacity (below); hiring is blocked on nothing at all — there is no command, no intent and no control, and the method it would call is finished.

## 2. Export downloads a file the application cannot read back

```
$ git grep -n "importInto" origin/main -- src
src/persistence/session/session-controller.ts:306:  public async importInto(prisonId: string, raw: unknown): Promise<SaveResult> {
```

One hit: the definition. `SessionController.importInto` is written, returns a `SaveResult`, and **nothing calls it**. Export is wired and reachable; import is not. A player can download a save file and has no way to load it.

This one is worth treating as a release concern rather than a feature: the save envelope is versioned and every shipped version stays loadable, and an import path is what makes that guarantee observable to a player instead of only to the test suite. It also gets harder the longer it waits, because each new persisted field widens the migration surface an importer has to survive.

## Why this is filed now

I put a research brief describing the codebase's measured state to four different models independently, asking what to build. **All four missed both of these**, despite the brief stating outright that export cannot be imported. One of the four listed "reloading an exported save file and resuming" as a requirement for a player's second session and then did not propose building it.

Three of the four also proposed hiring or deploying a guard as an activation step without noticing that nothing can hire one.

That is not a criticism of the models so much as a note about this defect class: **a missing producer is close to invisible from the outside.** The code reads as complete, the tests pass, and only tracing from the composition root outward shows nothing calls it. `tests/foundation/unconsumed-command-contract.test.ts` catches this for declared commands and is the reason `PurchaseMaterials` and `ZoneRoom` are on the record at all; neither of the two above is a command, so no gate sees them. A gate in the shape of `unreachable-invariant-contract.test.ts` — an exported capability with no production call site must be listed with a reason — would have caught both.

## Not this issue

**Room capacity is a separate and larger problem, already recorded on #261.** Worth stating here because all four models conflated it with zoning: giving a player the `ZoneRoom` producer does **not** admit a prisoner. `RoomZoningService.zone` registers an instance with `capacity: 0` and `objectCapabilities: []` (`src/simulation/rooms/zoning.ts:259-260`), and `RoomInstanceRegistry.findAvailable` rejects any instance where `occupancyOf(instanceId) >= instance.capacity` (`room-instance-registry.ts:81-87`) — which `0 >= 0` always satisfies. So zoning converts `IntakeSystem`'s `'failed'` into a retry-able backlog wait (`intake-system.ts:124-135`), and no prisoner is housed.

`zoning.ts:48-66` already says why, and says it is deliberate: capacity comes from the objects standing in a room, object placement does not exist (`docs/HUD_PROJECTIONS.md` gap 13), and *"giving a zoned room a usable capacity before object placement exists needs a content addition — the smallest being one authored occupancy figure per room definition — and that is a product decision."*

So the critical path to a housed prisoner is **object placement, or one authored occupancy figure per room type** — not the zoning gesture. That decision belongs on #261.

## Related

- #89 — the `PurchaseMaterials` producer, the same shape, closed by the buy surface.
- #261 — the reachability audit; room capacity and the `ZoneRoom` producer live there.
- #285 — the treasury has no reachable credit path, the same shape on the economy axis.
- ADR 0022 — records the zoning surface, and records the capacity finding rather than claiming it admits a prisoner.
