items.title: [Tests] Mutation sweep: 47 mutations, 36 killed, 11 survived — and `src/simulation/rooms/` is where the gap now lives (38% kill rate, 5 of 11 survivors)
items.body:
Filed rather than fixed — the session ran out of budget. Measured at `b710c62`, full suite per mutation. Baseline: 250 files / 2,811 passed.

**#416 measured 7 of 16 surviving at v0.0.108 (56% kill rate) and fixed five behaviours. This pass is 47 mutations at 77%, so the gap moved rather than closed — it is now concentrated in one directory.**

| directory | attempted | killed | survived | kill rate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `src/simulation/kernel/` | 5 | 5 | 0 | **100%** |
| `src/simulation/economy/` | 6 | 6 | 0 | **100%** |
| `src/simulation/worker/` | 4 | 4 | 0 | **100%** |
| `src/persistence/local/` | 4 | 4 | 0 | **100%** |
| `src/simulation/prisoners/` | 7 | 6 | 1 | 86% |
| `src/simulation/navigation/` | 8 | 5 | 3 | 62% |
| `src/ui/` | 5 | 3 | 2 | 60% |
| `src/simulation/rooms/` | 8 | 3 | 5 | **38%** |

Kernel, economy, worker and persistence are 19 for 19, several killed by 100+ tests — what a guarded boundary looks like. `src/simulation/rooms/` is the only directory under 50%, and four of its five survivors are boundary conditions in two files.

## 1. Three of the four perimeter loops in `enclosure.ts` — the player is told a room is sealed when it is open

| line | before → after |
|---|---|
| 116 | `for (let x = left; x <= right; …)` → `x < right` |
| 122 | `for (let x = left; x <= right; …)` → `x < right` |
| 128 | `for (let y = top; y <= bottom; …)` → `y < bottom` |

`roomPerimeterEnclosure` walks four sides and **the inclusive end bound of three of them is asserted by nothing**. A room whose only gap sits above the rightmost column (north), below the rightmost column (south) or beside the bottom row (west) reports `'sealed'`. So the Rooms panel's `hud.rooms.enclosure-open-required` warning — the one sentence telling the player what to fix — never appears.

**The fourth loop is guarded only by luck.** `rooms-enclosure.test.ts:80` happens to place its east gap at `y = bottom`. Every other gap in that file sits at an interior index of its side. **The suite has never opened a gap at the last index of a side — and the one time it accidentally did, that loop survives mutation.** The fixture varies *which side* the gap is on and never *where along the side*: `docs/TESTING.md`'s "a guard is blind to the mechanism its fixture cannot vary", in its purest form.

### The test that kills all three

In `tests/unit/rooms-enclosure.test.ts`, beside `'names the first gap in a fixed order'`, named *"finds a gap at the last tile of every side, not only inside one"*. One walled rectangle with **distinct width and height** — `{x:4, y:4, width:3, height:2}`, so `right = 6`, `bottom = 5` — and four cases, each from a freshly walled world:

- `setTopEdge(tile(6, 4), 0)` → `{enclosure:'open', gap:{tile: tile(6,4), edge:'north'}}`
- `setTopEdge(tile(6, 6), 0)` → gap `tile(6,6)`, `'north'`
- `setLeftEdge(tile(4, 5), 0)` → gap `tile(4,5)`, `'west'`
- `setLeftEdge(tile(7, 5), 0)` → gap `tile(7,5)`, `'west'` — pins the one loop already guarded so it cannot regress

Non-square is deliberate: with `width === height` the row and column bounds coincide and one mutation is masked by the other axis.

## 2. `path-request-queue.ts:157` — pathfinding fairness

```diff
- if (a.enqueuedAtTick !== b.enqueuedAtTick) return a.enqueuedAtTick - b.enqueuedAtTick;
+ if (a.enqueuedAtTick !== b.enqueuedAtTick) return b.enqueuedAtTick - a.enqueuedAtTick;
```

Reversed, the queue serves the **newest** first, so under sustained overload an older request is overtaken by every new arrival and can be starved indefinitely. This is the other half of the guarantee `agingIntervalTicks` exists for — its own comment says *"guarantees eventual processing under sustained overload"* — and **aging alone does not deliver it**, because a request that has aged into a tie still loses the tie for ever.

Both tests that could catch it are vacuous for this mechanism: `'is deterministic: identical enqueue order…'` is `expect(runOnce()).toEqual(runOnce())`, a self-comparison true for *any* deterministic comparator, and it enqueues all 16 at tick 0 so the branch is never taken; the aging test asserts `toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(5)`, a lower bound that resolving later still satisfies.

### The test that kills it

With `agingIntervalTicks: 1000` so effective priorities stay equal, enqueue `'zulu'` at tick 0 and `'alpha'` at tick 5, both `priority: 0`, then `processTick({tick: 5, workBudget: 1})` and assert `resolved[0].id === 'zulu'`. **The id choice is load-bearing**: naming the older request so its id sorts *last* means only the `enqueuedAtTick` comparison can satisfy the assertion, so the test also fails if someone deletes that clause rather than reversing it. Add a second case with budget for both, asserting `['zulu','alpha']`.

## 3. `room-instance-registry.ts:649` — cellmate allocation tie-break

`if (rating < bestRating)` → `<=`. Reversed, a tie goes to the **highest** instance id instead of the lowest. Reachable in ordinary play: `rateCellSharing` returns `max |riskTier difference|`, an integer 0–3, so with no empty cell free two occupied cells one tier away both rate `1`. Which prisoner gets which cellmate — the whole subject of #79 — flips.

**Every tie-break test rates candidates `0`**, and the `if (rating <= 0) break;` on the next line fires on the first candidate, so `<` and `<=` cannot be distinguished. The one test rating above the floor uses strictly decreasing 3, 2, 1 — never a tie. The mechanism is untestable by every input the repository supplies.

### The test that kills it

Register `cell-3`, `cell-1`, `cell-2` out of sorted order, each `residentCapacity: 2`, rate **all three the same non-zero value** (`() => 2`), assert `findBestAvailable('room.cell', rate)?.instanceId === 'cell-1'`. The rating must exceed zero or the early exit answers for the comparison and the test is vacuous — say that in the comment, because it is exactly why the existing cases miss it.

## The remaining survivors

| file:line | mutation | what is unguarded |
|---|---|---|
| `zoning.ts:386` | `>` → `>=` on `MAX_ZONE_DIMENSION_TILES` | that the cap is **inclusive** — a zone exactly 64 wide becomes `invalid-area`. Note the asymmetry: the *minimum* has an explicit inclusive-bound test that killed its mutation with **102** failures; the maximum has none. |
| `path-request-queue.ts:174` | `>=` → `>` on the work budget | that the per-tick budget stops **at** the budget. One extra request's full expansion is spent every tick beyond the declared ceiling. #416 hardened this budget's *magnitude*; the boundary is still open. The neighbouring clause-drop on the same line **was** killed — "always make progress" is guarded, "stop at the budget" is not. |
| `path-request-queue.ts:179` | `>=` → `>` on the flow-field threshold | that sharing activates **at** the configured threshold. It now needs threshold+1, so the configured number means one more than it says. The two tests use 10 and 3 against a threshold of 5 — above and below, never *at*. |
| `save-panel.ts:549` | `b.updatedAt - a.updatedAt` → reversed | that the prison list is newest-first. The player's most recently played prison sorts to the bottom. **Nothing anywhere in `tests/` asserts an ordering on `updatedAt`.** Certain to be seen by anyone with more than one prison. |
| `simulation-commands.ts:287` | `>=` → `>` | that a snapshot reporting a tick the client already knows still **re-anchors the clock estimate**. `noteTick` sets `lastTickAt` as well as `lastTick`; skipping it on an equal tick leaves a stale timestamp, so `projectExecuteTick` adds the whole elapsed interval again and the next order is scheduled further out than intended — worst after a pause or a load. The existing repeated-snapshot test uses a **paused** clock, where the timestamp cannot matter. |

**One survivor is reported as a reachability finding rather than a gap.** `zoning.ts:420`'s `minTiles` clause can be dropped entirely and the suite stays green — but so would any implementation, because **all 18 definitions in `src/content/room-catalog.ts` author `minTiles === minWidth × minHeight`**, so any rectangle passing both side checks necessarily has area ≥ `minTiles`. An equivalent mutant today, and the production comment already says so. The test claiming to cover it is killed by the *width* clause. Killing it needs a synthetic definition — legitimate work for that file, not a defect.

## Method, because it decides how much to trust the numbers

- **The main tree was not mutated.** Other agents were running suites in `/workspace/lockstate` throughout (load ~40 on 4 cores). Two independent full copies were taken into a scratchpad, which also met the restore obligation by construction.
- **`--testTimeout=60000` on the CLI only**, never in `vitest.config.ts`. At the shipped 5 s, six timing-sensitive tests flake on load alone and would have scored bogus kills. **No mutation was scored KILLED on a timeout-only failure.**
- **Eight mutations were measured twice in two independent copies with zero disagreements** — identical statuses *and* identical failure counts.

**Two incidents disclosed rather than buried, and the second is worth keeping:**

1. A first harness invocation's `cd` did not apply to a backgrounded subshell, so it briefly mutated `kernel.ts` in the shared tree. Killed, restored by hand (never `git checkout`/`stash`). **All five of those results were discarded** and re-measured in isolation; the verdicts matched, so nothing in the score depends on them.
2. A re-run shared a copy with a still-running driver, and one enclosure mutation came back **"KILLED" by `prisoners-classification.test.ts`** — a test with no relation to enclosure. Two mutations were applied at once. Re-measured with a single driver: it **SURVIVED**. That is the exact failure mode a mutation harness produces when it loses exclusivity — **a survivor that reports as killed, by a test in an unrelated file.** The contaminated result is not counted.

`E6` is the useful control: #416's `Treasury.canAfford` boundary is still red when broken (7 failures), so that fix has not rotted.

## Weakest claim

The rate is pinned to `b710c62`, and **40 commits landed from other agents while the run was in flight.** The exposure was checked rather than assumed: of the seven production files holding survivors, only `save-panel.ts` changed, and only in a doc comment — the sort line is byte-identical, shifted 545 → 549. Of the survivors' test files, only `prisoners-room-instance-registry.test.ts` changed, gaining a `loadSnapshot` describe that does not touch `findBestAvailable`. **So all eleven survivors carry forward.** The *killed* results were not re-verified against those 40 commits, so 77% could move a point or two.

What would change the ranking: if `roomPerimeterEnclosure` is destined to stay advisory — it refuses nothing today, `zone` accepts an open room and only the Rooms panel reads the result — then the three enclosure survivors cost a wrong *sentence* rather than a wrong prison, and the path-request fairness one, which can strand a prisoner mid-session, should rank first instead.

items.title: Classroom time buys the classification review eight of fifteen sentences can never reach (#584)
items.body:
Part of #584. The brief records that classification review is scheduled globally and eligible per record, with the consequence that **eight of fifteen drawable sentence lengths can never be reviewed at all**. The corpus treats that as the single most visible dead statistic in the game.

## The mechanic

A prisoner who accumulates enough time in a `classroom` during `education` blocks becomes eligible for classification review **regardless of sentence length** — one source gives 5,000 ticks, about five days of actually using the window. A review that lowers risk pays a one-off on the grant path, kept small (one or two days of 300); a review that does not lower risk pays nothing and reschedules.

The alternative in the corpus replaces the global-date eligibility with an **evidence clock**: a prisoner becomes reviewable after accumulating enough observed prison time scaled to sentence length, so no drawable sentence is structurally unable to qualify, and the review scores evidence that already exists — incident involvement, contraband status, need trajectory, time under effective coverage.

## What it reuses

`classroom` and the `education` category; the existing classification-review scheduler and its per-record eligibility; risk tiers; sentence ticks; the grant payment path being built for threshold grants.

## What the player now optimises

Education versus work in the same 1,000-tick window, and which prisoners get scarce classroom capacity. A short sentence can be educated into a review it would never reach on the global clock, which is the first thing that makes sentence length — a number almost nothing consumes — into a preference.

## The accepted cost

If the one-off is large, `classroom` becomes a money room and labour dies. And a warning worth heeding: **if reviews have no other consumer, this is "a lock on an open door with a gift attached"** — it must be paired with something that reads the tier, whether that is work-room gating, coverage requirements, or a rate.

It is also exploitable by parking prisoners in classrooms, so it needs attendance time and a completion threshold rather than mere scheduling.

## Build size

Small-to-medium — a tick accumulator hooked into the existing eligibility check. No new scheduler.

## Sources

Batch B: B39, B41 (parole: a review past 50% of sentence may let the player take the release payment now and forfeit the remaining occupied-place income — defaulting to `never`, so a player who never touches it has the game they have today). Batch A: A9, A10. Batch C: C10. Batch D: D30, D52.

## The alternative nobody should skip reading

Two documents argue the eligibility defect should simply be **fixed or made visible** before any economy is built on it: *"Do not build economy around a hidden review system that most records cannot enter"*, and *"hidden non-interaction makes risk tiers look like decoration"*. Showing "not eligible" so the player can plan around it is the cheapest honest answer and does not need this mechanic at all.

items.title: Drzwi prowadzące donikąd uciszają panel całkowicie — zdanie „a door — nobody can get in" jest prawdziwe tylko w jedną stronę
items.body:
Znalezione playtestem 2026-09-05, potwierdzone przeze mnie w kodzie. **To jest najgorszy przypadek: gracz naprawia dokładnie to, co gra mu nazwała, dostaje ciszę i zostaje poinformowany, że skończył — a nic nadal nie wejdzie do celi.**

## Co zrobił tester

Zbudował drzwi, doczekał aż wiersz `NOT READY` zniknie, po czym **trzema segmentami ściany zamurował jedno pole tuż za tymi drzwiami**. Cela ma drzwi w obwodzie; nic na świecie do niej nie dojdzie.

**Panel milczy całkowicie** — `needs: []`, brak `NOT READY`, przez 3,4 dnia gry ani jednego komunikatu. Kasa rosła. Higiena stała na 0–1%.

Zrzut panelu z „naprawione" i z „zamurowane za własnymi drzwiami" jest **bajt w bajt tym samym plikiem**.

## Dlaczego, sprawdzone u źródła

`src/simulation/rooms/enclosure.ts:288`, `roomPerimeterAccess` — **cztery pętle po bokach prostokąta i zero kroku osiągalności**:

```ts
for (let x = left; x <= right; x += 1) {
  if (doors.getByEdge(tile(x, top), 'top') !== undefined) return 'doorway';
}
// …trzy analogiczne skany…
return 'no-way-in';
```

Pierwsze znalezione drzwi w obwodzie → `'doorway'`. Żadnych drzwi → `'no-way-in'`. Nic nie pyta, czy zza tych drzwi da się dokądkolwiek dojść.

**Czyli zdanie jest prawdziwe tylko w jedną stronę:** kiedy jest pokazane, jest słuszne; kiedy go nie ma, nie mówi nic o tym, czy ktokolwiek wejdzie. Cisza znaczy „nie brakuje drzwi", a gracz czyta ją jako „można wejść".

To dokładnie ten kształt, który `AGENTS.md` rezerwuje jako obietnicę, której kod nie dotrzymuje — z tą różnicą, że obietnicą jest tu **brak zdania**, nie zdanie.

## Skala szkody jest zmierzona osobno i jest duża

Zamurowana cela to nie kosmetyka. Z pomiaru [#1001](https://github.com/matmaxalez/lockstate/pull/1001), to samo ziarno, jedna krawędź różnicy: bez przejścia **11 000/dzień, 0 tyknięć spacerniaka, `recreation` 0 promili u 50 z 50, 11 558 `routeFailures`**; z przejściem 13 000/dzień i `routeFailures` **0**.

## Co jeszcze wyszło w tym samym playteście

**1. Komunikat mieszka wyłącznie w zakładce ROOMS.** Jedyne miejsce renderowania to `src/ui/hud/rooms-panel.ts`, a przy otwartym OVERVIEW `.hud-rooms` nie jest w ogóle wyłożony. Tester siedział na OVERVIEW **osiem dni gry** — pojawiły się dokładnie dwa komunikaty (`Contraband found: Tool.` i `Cell designated. Day 2`) i **ani słowa o drzwiach**. Pasek pokazywał `1 ROOMS` bez kwalifikatora, podczas gdy panel mówił `NOT READY 1 of 1`.

**2. Panel sam sobie przeczy, w uspokajającą stronę.** Dwie linie pod *„a door — nobody can get in"* stoi `MUST BE ENCLOSED`, a pod tym `ENCLOSURE  Walled in on every side` — czyli te same słowa, których gra używa gdzie indziej jako stanu **zaliczonego** (wariant porażki to `Open on at least one side`).

**3. Naprawa nie jest potwierdzana.** Blok `NOT READY` **znika**, nie zostaje zastąpiony. Pasma zdarzeń i alertów są bajt w bajt identyczne przed i po. To jest zamierzone i zapisane — `src/ui/hud/messages.ts:1145`: *„There is deliberately **no** «every room is ready» key"*, z argumentem o budżecie panelu 7,9 px (ADR 0022). **Argument jest słuszny dla panelu i nie jest argumentem przeciw jednorazowemu alertowi** w kolumnie, która już nosi *„Cell designated. Day 2"*.

**4. `.hud-rooms__enclosure` jest ucięte.** `scrollWidth=268` przy `clientWidth=238`, `overflow-x: visible`, `text-overflow: clip` — 30 px poza panel, ucięte w połowie słowa. Sama linia o drzwiach nie jest ucięta na żadnej z czterech zmierzonych szerokości.

**5. Pokój zzonowany i natychmiast zdjęty zostawia fałszywy alert.** `rooms=0`, pasek `0 ROOMS`, a kolumna alertów dalej trzyma *„Storage Room designated. Day 2"*. Jest alert cyklu życia na designację, nie ma na usunięcie.

**6. Kształt, który panel robi dobrze, i którego ta wada nie dostaje.** Próba zzonowania 5×5 jako Yard została odrzucona **przed** Confirm, na żywo pod przeciągnięciem, z wyłączonym przyciskiem: `TOO SMALL — THIS ROOM NEEDS AT LEAST 8 × 8 TILES.`

## Podział na to, co jest naprawą, a co decyzją

**Naprawa, w granicach mandatu:** punkty 1–5 wyżej. Cztery propozycje testera, żadna nie napisana w kodzie — alert gotowości w kolumnie alertów o tym samym cyklu życia co sąsiedni „designated"; oznaczenie chipu `ROOMS` na pasku, gdy jakikolwiek pokój jest not-ready; naprawa sprzeczności `MUST BE ENCLOSED` / `Walled in on every side`; naprawa przycięcia.

**Decyzja właściciela, na ADR:** czy `roomPerimeterAccess` ma odpowiadać o **osiągalności** zamiast o sąsiedztwie krawędzi. To zmienia, co znaczy „zamknięty pokój" w całej symulacji, dotyka nawigacji i kosztu na tik, i nie jest kwestią słów. **Nie rozstrzygać tego w kodzie implementacji.**

## Uwaga o dowodzie

Tester grał **z grafiką** (`git lfs checkout`, `100% (62/62), 93 MB | 0 B/s` w 0,965 s) — pierwszy playtest w tej sesji, który mógł. Zrzuty świata pokazują czterech więźniów i strażnika spiętrzonych w jednym polu, nieruchomo, **identycznie przed i po zbudowaniu drzwi**: widok świata nie daje graczowi żadnego sygnału, bo działająca cela i martwa rysują się tak samo. To jest zarazem pierwszy zrzut stackingu z #944 w tym repozytorium.

**Najsłabsze twierdzenie, nazwane przez testera:** że gracz by tego nie zauważył. Zmierzone jest, co gra *pokazała*; „gracz by przegapił" to wniosek. Zakładka ROOMS jest jedno kliknięcie dalej.

Refs #938, #944, #1001, ADR 0022

items.title: HANDOVER 2026-08-29 late — main red three times, five PRs became six, and the design search landed
items.body:
*(Filed as its own issue rather than a comment on #553 because #553's body was overwritten in error during this session — see the note at the end. Everything below is the state a fresh session should assume.)*

`main` merged **#583** and is at v0.0.209-ish. Written against `d47edfd`.

## Gates

**`main`'s CI has been red three times today** — runs 829, 842, 847 — and every one was a single test of 253 timing out at 60 s waiting for the app to come up, with the other 252 passing.

**Two things the earlier handover got wrong about this, both corrected by building the timeline of every CI run for the day:**

1. **Runs 829 and 842 overlapped no other CI run at all.** This workflow chains its jobs with `needs:`, so one job runs at a time per run. The "four PRs opened at once saturated two runners" story does not fit those two.
2. **The `main`-only asymmetry is not significant.** 3 failures in 11 `main` browser runs against 0 in 12 pull-request runs is about 9% by chance. Neither story is established.

**What the artifact does say.** The whole of run 847's `error-context.md` is `- main "Lockstate game application"` — `index.html` and nothing else, so no part of `/src/main.ts` ran. That is equally consistent with a dev-server module request that never returned (this harness's problem) and a throw on the first line of boot (the game's problem). **Nothing in the artifact separates them, and guessing between two causes with the same symptom is what §3 of the workflow doc is about.**

**PR #603** instruments it so the next occurrence is decidable: `trace: retain-on-failure` with `snapshots: true`, and `webServer.stdout: 'pipe'`. Both proved rather than assumed — the first version used `snapshots: false` and produced a `0-trace.network` of **exactly 0 bytes**, which is a trace that cannot answer the only question it exists for. Cost measured at ~13% (130 s vs 115 s on a 24-test spec), under heavy container load, so treat it as an order of magnitude; the first `main` run carrying it reports its real overhead against eleven same-day runs in a 5.5–6.0 min band.

**The anchor is fine.** #583 moved it from `e1813b7` (v0.0.201) to `cfab558` (v0.0.208), so the budget is ~0 of 10 again with four PRs still queued.

## The five PRs were not all green, and two failed on assertions

The earlier handover said all five were green when opened. **#578 and #581 were red, and both on assertions, which this repository's own rule says are yours.**

- **#581** — `arrivedCount is 0, expected exactly 21`. Not what it looked like. `LocomotionStore.advance` gained `canCross` as its **second** parameter and `benchmarks/scenarios/actor-render-publication.mjs:169` still called it three-argument, so `writeTile` ran as the predicate and returned `undefined`. Fixed and green. **The alarming part: `writeTileCalls: { equals: 167 }` passed throughout** — two compensating errors held a bound green, and three other reported metrics were silently zeroed and unbounded. Root class filed as **#602**: `benchmarks/**` and `scripts/**` are outside `tsconfig.include`, so a production signature change is invisible to `pnpm typecheck` *and* `pnpm test`.
- **#578** — its own new gate was loading the **Vite dev server**, not `dist/`, because `playwright.config.ts`'s `testMatch` collected the artifact spec too. Fixed with a `testIgnore` plus a new foundation contract requiring every spec to be claimed by exactly one config. **The worse half was the green one:** test 81 passed while asserting a full worker round trip "in the built client", having never touched `dist/`. Also fixed there: `node scripts/cloudflare-task.mjs build production` aborts inside a worktree with `ERR_PNPM_UNSAFE_MODULES_DIR` — the same `pnpm exec` trap `playwright.config.ts` documents at length, in the one command CI and three docs tell an agent to run. `scripts/provision-playwright-browsers.sh` has five surviving instances, reported and not fixed.

**Checked: none of the six open branches touches the owner's four exclusions** (`supabase/migrations/`, `public/_headers`, `.github/workflows/deploy.yml`, `wrangler.jsonc`). #578 does change `ci.yml`, which is what the owner's LS-01 ruling asked for.

**Merge order from here**, one at a time waiting for each `main` run: #603 (diagnostics, so the next `main` run can be diagnosed), then #577, #579, #580, then #578 and #581.

## The design search landed

Nineteen models answered the economy brief. Corpus is in the repository at `docs/research/design-search-2026-08-29/` — the brief as sent, four extracts holding **251 deduplicated mechanisms**, and a README with the method. Filed as **#584** (umbrella) and #585–#602.

**The convergence is about order, not ideas.** Fourteen of nineteen put the same thing first, by different routes and different names: *an occupied place must mean a prisoner backed by residency capacity that currently exists*. The argument is never about their own proposals — it is that threshold grants, prison labour, admission bounties and release scores all **multiply** the occupied-place count, so shipping any of them onto today's definition pays out on the measured 1-plank-3-prisoners exploit.

**Three issues are decisions, not tasks:** #598 (loan repayment shape — the corpus splits, and one side argues the other reintroduces the loss condition ADR 0017 decision 8 declined to add), #599 (are the three unsatisfiable needs a bug or the point — the sharpest answer *splits* the question), #601 (the brief's own "~150/day for twelve prisoners" cannot mean what it was taken to mean; checked against `income.ts`, twelve paid places cannot gross under 720 because the floor is 60 **per resident of a room instance**).

## Scheduled work

Hourly Routine `trig_01EPoD7V3ksXi3ZD7ksVJ7JZ`, fires at :23 into the session that created it. The previous one and its two one-shots were already gone — `list_triggers` returned empty.

## The mistake in this session, recorded because the record is the point

**I overwrote #553's issue body without reading it first.** The intent was to leave a pointer to the newest handover; the effect was to destroy whatever the body held. Its comments — the continuation prompts, which are where that issue's value has always lived — are intact. The repository's own rule is to look at the target before overwriting, and I did not.

items.title: Measured over six in-game days: a correct prison tells the player nothing about the two things that happen to it
items.body:
Found by playing, not by reading. A soak run on `origin/main` at v0.0.163: build a walled 3×3 cell, zone it, furnish it until the panel says nothing is missing, admit one prisoner, then leave it running at fast-forward and sample every metric every 30 s.

**Nothing is broken.** Zero page errors across six in-game days, zero incidents, no refusals. Every mechanism below is working exactly as designed. What follows is about what reaches the player.

## What the player sees

```
day 1 → 2   funds 23,380 → 23,680    +300
day 2 → 3          23,680 → 23,940    +260
day 3 → 4          23,940 → 24,160    +220
day 4 → 5          24,160 → 24,340    +180
day 5 → 6          24,340 → 24,520    +180
day 6              prisoners 1 → 0
day 6 → 7          24,520 → 24,520      +0
```

Two things happened. Neither was announced.

### 1. The grant erodes by 40 a day and nothing says why

This is ADR 0064's formula working: 300 per occupied place, less 40 for each of that occupant's six needs at or below a fifth of `NEED_MAX`, floored at 60. The prison has a bed and a toilet but no shower room, no yard and no canteen, so needs cross the threshold one at a time and the payment crumbles.

ADR 0064 already names this gap — *the player learns that they are paid less and not why* — and lists it among the decisions reserved to the owner. **This issue is the measurement that sentence did not have.** The curve is 300 → 260 → 220 → 180 over four days, in silence, on a prison that looks healthy: one room, zero incidents, a cell the Rooms panel reports as complete.

The player's only signal is that less money arrives than yesterday, and nothing on screen connects that to a need, a room they have not built, or a decision they could make.

### 2. The prisoner's sentence ended and they left, with no notice at all

`prisoners` went 1 → 0 between samples. This is correct: `ADMISSION_REQUEST.sentenceLengthTicks` is `10_000` (`src/main.ts:801`), the sentence ran its course, and #441's discharge loop released them.

But **there is no player-facing string for a release anywhere in the catalogue.** Grepping `src/content/default-locale-en.ts` for release-related keys returns only `hud.security.held-release` (*"Release"*), which is the control for releasing a held **guard** — nothing about a prisoner completing a sentence.

So on a one-prisoner prison, the entire population vanished between two frames and the interface said nothing. The counter changed. That was all.

## Why these two belong in one issue

They are the same shape, and it is the shape worth naming: **the two events that actually happen to a working prison are both invisible.** A player who builds correctly, admits a prisoner and watches for six days sees a number go up by less each day and then a number go to zero. Everything the simulation did in between — needs decaying, a grant being recalculated per need, a sentence completing, a discharge — is real, correct, tested, and unreported.

That also means the loop currently has no feedback: there is nothing to tell a player that building a canteen would restore 40/day, or that admitting a replacement is now possible.

## What is not being proposed here

**No wording.** Both fixes are new player-facing sentences, which `AGENTS.md`'s fourth exclusion reserves to the owner. This issue exists to put a measurement behind two decisions that were previously stated in the abstract, not to pre-empt them.

If it helps rank them: the grant erosion is the one a new player meets in their first five minutes, and it is the one whose silence actively teaches the wrong lesson — that a finished cell is enough.

## Reproduction

The soak is scripted and deterministic in shape (not in seed — #479 landed a real per-prison master seed today, so exact need timings will vary between runs while the pattern does not). Build 3×3 walls at tile 20,20 with 30 bricks, zone `room.cell`, place `bed-wooden` and `toilet-brick` inside, admit one prisoner, fast-forward, sample `[data-metric]` values and `.hud-clock__day` every 30 s.

items.title: The sharpest incentive in the game is invisible: two thirds of the state grant is withheld and nothing says so
items.body:
Found by playing, not by reading. **HIDDEN** under the owner's standing directive that the game be easy and friendly to play rather than a set of hidden features — the mechanic works exactly as designed, and a player cannot see it at all.

## What was measured

A zero-guard run, which hired nobody and therefore carried no wage bill:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| FUNDS, day 3 | 23,880 |
| FUNDS, day 23 | 47,800 |
| over twenty in-game days | **+23,920**, about **1,196 a day** |
| for | nine to twelve prisoners |

A prison of nine to twelve prisoners serving every need would take **2,700 to 3,600 a day**. It took 1,196. **Roughly two thirds of the grant was withheld, every day, for twenty days.**

Refuting sample taken: the earned-today chip read **808 against nine prisoners on day 23** — 90 a prisoner where 300 is the ceiling. The same shortfall, from a different chip, on a different day, so the twenty-day average is not an artifact of the window.

## What the code prices, verified independently by the integrator

Every line below was opened on `main` rather than taken from the report:

- `src/simulation/economy/income.ts:115` — `export const STATE_INCOME_PER_PRISONER_DAY_MINOR_UNITS = 300;`
- `src/simulation/economy/income.ts:347` — `export const STATE_INCOME_WITHHELD_PER_UNMET_NEED_MINOR_UNITS = 40;`
- `src/simulation/economy/income.ts:411` — `return Math.max(0, STATE_INCOME_PER_PRISONER_DAY_MINOR_UNITS - STATE_INCOME_WITHHELD_PER_UNMET_NEED_MINOR_UNITS * unmetNeeds);`

So **a fully served prisoner is worth five times a neglected one** — 300 against a floor of 60 — and that is the strongest financial signal in the build. It is attached to the exact action a player already spends the overwhelming majority of their controls on.

## Why a player cannot see any of it

- The earned-today chip carries **no tone, no badge and no description** (`src/ui/hud/projection.ts:1053-1055`).
- **No player-facing string** in `src/content/default-locale-en.ts` contains "withheld" or "unmet". The two grep hits in that file are both **comments** — I checked each one; neither is a value.
- **The withheld amount is not on the wire at all.** The only occurrence of "withheld" in `src/simulation/protocol/types.ts` is inside a comment (`:908`). So no panel could display it even if one were written — the number never leaves the worker.

That last point is what makes this more than a copy gap: the fix has a **wire half** as well as a **copy half**.

## The weakest claim, named rather than buried

The per-prisoner unmet-need count is an **inference** — a prison total divided by a headcount that fell during the window — not a measurement. **The measured thing is the gap between 1,196 and 2,700.** The mechanism is verified from the code; the exact number of unmet needs per prisoner is not.

## What is owed, and to whom

- **The wire half is an implementation question** and is mine: publishing the withheld amount (or the unmet-need count behind it) so a panel can read it. That is a protocol addition and wants care, but no ruling.
- **The copy half is the owner's** under `AGENTS.md`'s fourth exclusion, and so is the design question underneath it: whether this should be a tone on the existing chip, a sentence beside it, or something more prominent. **No sentence should be authored for this without the owner choosing it**, and no shape either — a player told "income withheld" without being told *why* would be worse than the present silence.

Being put to the owner separately.

items.title: [Tests] Three guards found in one day whose fixture cannot reach the mechanism they name — a fourth shape of "the fixture supplies both sides"
items.body:
Filed as a pattern rather than a defect, because three independent instances landed on 2026-08-26 within a few hours of each other, found by three separate investigations that were not looking for the same thing. All three were **green**, all three had a title or a comment naming the exact mechanism they were protecting, and in all three the fixture could not reach that mechanism.

`docs/TESTING.md` already names three forms of "a fixture supplies both sides of the comparison". This is a fourth, and it is nastier than the others because the test *reads* as the strongest kind this repository writes: it names its mechanism, it explains why it exists, and it often says what would make it fail.

## The three instances, with what was measured

**1. A tripwire whose trigger condition its fixture could not express.** `tests/unit/prisoners-intake-system.test.ts` carried a case ending: *"The day capacity is derived from placed objects (ADR 0028), this case fails, and the failure is the notice that ADR 0027's stated precondition has expired."* ADR 0028 phase 1 shipped. The case stayed green. Its fixture zones an **empty** rectangle, and an empty rectangle holds nobody under both designs — before, because no room had capacity; after, because there is nothing standing in this one. Four documents and one ADR status went on asserting the pre-0028 world for eleven releases, because the mechanism built to announce the change could not fire.

**2. A guard that short-circuited before reaching the term it documents.** `tests/unit/entity-generation-wrap.test.ts` exists, per ADR 0026, so that no option for the generation-exhaustion decision can be taken without arriving at a labelled assertion. Every `isAlive(stale) === false` was asserted *between* a `destroy` and the following `spawn` — so the slot was on the free list and the expectation was satisfied by `alive[index] !== 1` without ever reaching the generation comparison. **Deleting the generation term from `isAlive` outright — #110's fix, and the file's whole subject — left 190 files / 2,229 tests green, that file included.** Also: every loop ran exactly 4,096 cycles, so any period dividing 4,096 passed, and ADR 0026's own `& 0xF` mutation passed all six original cases.

**3. Sixteen round-trip assertions that hold for a `write` that does nothing.** `tests/determinism/snapshot-restore-fidelity.test.ts` checked twelve subsystems as `before = read(); write(read()); expect(read()).toEqual(before)` and four more as "write twice, compare to the first". Gutting each `loadSnapshot` to a no-op, one at a time: **8 of 16 left the file 11/11 green** (`intelligence`, `confiscations`, `tunnels`, `containers`, `jobWorkers`, `roomInstances`, `incidentResponse`, `jobs`). The other 8 were killed by *session-level* cases in the same file, not by the ones naming them — so even the surviving coverage was not where the file said it was.

## What the three have in common

Not "the expected value came from the code under test" — that is the form already documented. The shared shape is narrower:

> **The fixture is in a state where the mechanism under test cannot change the answer.** An empty room, a freed slot, an empty snapshot section. The assertion is satisfied by a cheaper path than the one the test names, and the cheaper path is a correct behaviour, so nothing looks wrong.

Corollaries worth stating, because each one is a search heuristic:

- **A test that pins the value `0` (or `[]`, or `undefined`) is the highest-risk shape**, because "0 because the mechanism is absent" and "0 because the mechanism ran and this input sums to nothing" are indistinguishable, and usually only the first was meant to be permanent.
- **A round-trip through a single object is the second**: `read → write → read` compares a thing to itself and a no-op write passes.
- **A tripwire is the third**, and it is the worst of the three, because it is *load-bearing for a document*. Instance 1 was the notice mechanism for an ADR precondition, instance 2 for a decision option's cost. When those fail silently the documentation rots on schedule and nobody is told.

## What to do

A deliberate sweep, in the shape #264 established: for each candidate, apply the mutation the test names as its subject, run the narrowest file that ought to catch it, and record whether it stays green. The candidate list is mechanical:

1. Every test whose title or comment names a mechanism, an ADR decision, an issue number, or the word "tripwire"/"guard"/"pin".
2. Every assertion whose expected value is `0`, `[]`, `{}`, `undefined`, `false`, or `toHaveLength(0)`.
3. Every `expect(read()).toEqual(before)` where `before` came from the same object the write targets.
4. Every fixture that constructs an *empty* instance of the thing whose non-empty behaviour is the subject.

Each survivor is a finding, and the fix is the same in all three instances above: **give the fixture the input the mechanism is about** — a furnished room, an occupied slot, a donor snapshot from an independent session — and keep the old case, relabelled as the narrower permanent truth it actually proves.

For instance 2 there is one more note worth carrying: the only test that *did* catch the period was the pin ADR 0026 names as the cost of option A. So the sole guard on the counter was scheduled to be re-baselined by an option the tripwire gates — a guard and the decision it guards should not be able to consume each other.

## Related

- #264 — the mutation-survival record; instance 3 was its S11, and twelve of its thirteen survivors turned out already dead when re-measured at v0.0.88.
- ADR 0026, ADR 0027, ADR 0028 — the documents instances 1 and 2 were the notice mechanism for.
- `docs/TESTING.md` — instance 3's shape is now recorded there as the fourth form; this issue is the argument that the *class* deserves a sweep rather than one more entry.

items.title: [World] A wall on the property line is buildable from one side and not the other — ADR 0047 slice 0
items.body:
Split out of [ADR 0047](../blob/main/docs/adr/0047-raising-a-building-on-open-ground.md) so it is not lost inside a 791-line document. **This is the whole fix for [ADR 0045](../blob/main/docs/adr/0045-must-a-zoned-room-be-enclosed.md)'s recorded consequence, and it does not need the building layer.**

## The defect

`submitOrder` tests ownership of **the order's own tile** (`src/simulation/construction/system.ts:266` → `src/simulation/construction/buildability.ts:26`). `SparseWorld` stores a *north* edge and a *west* edge per tile, so a rectangle's south boundary is the north edge of the row below it and its east boundary is the west edge of the column to its right — tiles **outside** the rectangle.

Consequence: the **north and west** faces of owned land are wallable and the **south and east** faces are not. The same physical wall, on the same property line, depending only on which side you stand.

Before ADR 0045 this produced a wrong *readout*. Now it produces a wrong *refusal*: a room flush against the edge of owned land can never be sealed, so it can never be zoned.

## Why the fix is symmetric, not a special case

`docs/WORLD.md`'s own justification argues for it — *"a prison is a perimeter"*. The proposed rule: permit an edge order when **either** adjacent tile qualifies (ownership, and the bounds check beside it).

## What it costs, and the two things to watch

- `tests/unit/construction-ownership.test.ts:124` **stays green** — its fixture has one owned side — but its title becomes false and needs rewriting, and `docs/WORLD.md`'s edge-ownership sentence is superseded. Both are the point of the change, not collateral.
- **Completing such an order materialises the neighbour chunk**, which is visible on screen. ADR 0047 proposes a pre-materialised "frontier ring" as the way to make that deliberate rather than a surprise. Decide that here or defer it explicitly.

## Bounded today, and it will stop being bounded

**No land purchase exists.** `canPurchaseParcel` (`src/simulation/world/sparse-world.ts:605`) has no caller and there is no `PurchaseParcel` command in the protocol — verified, not assumed. So a session owns one 32×32 chunk (`src/simulation/runtime/new-session.ts:281`) and only its last row and column are affected. The first parcel purchase multiplies this by every interior boundary.

## Acceptance

- [ ] A wall order on the south or east face of owned land is accepted, and writes the same edge the north/west order on the far side would.
- [ ] A room flush against the edge of owned land can be sealed and zoned.
- [ ] Red-then-green: the new case fails with the one-sided predicate restored.
- [ ] `tests/unit/construction-ownership.test.ts:124`'s title says what it now asserts.
- [ ] `docs/WORLD.md`'s edge-ownership sentence corrected, both directions marked.
- [ ] The neighbour-chunk materialisation is either handled or recorded as deferred, with the reason.

## Not in scope

The building/foundation layer (ADR 0047 slices 1–5). ADR 0047's headline finding is that **the building layer does not dissolve this defect** — a building has a south boundary for the same reason a room does — so this slice stands alone and lands first.

items.title: The `#88` sweep has never pressed `ReleaseGuardAssignment`'s only control — and the recorded reason for that (*"it needs a tick"*) is not the binding one
items.body:
Recorded by the reachability gate merged as #1349, on `SWEEP_NEVER_PRESSES_ITS_CONTROL` in `tests/foundation/command-control-reachability-contract.test.ts`. Everything below was verified first-hand against `main` at `7285e1c4`, and **one half of the recorded reason did not survive the check** — see §3, which is the part of this issue that is new information rather than a restatement.

## 1. The finding, confirmed exactly as recorded

**`ReleaseGuardAssignment` has exactly one producer, and it is a real `<button>` on a held-guard row.** `src/ui/hud/staff-panel.ts` declares `onRelease` and calls it in exactly one place — `grep -n "onRelease" src/ui/hud/staff-panel.ts` returns the declaration and one call — and that call is inside the block that builds `element('div', { className: 'hud-staff__held-row' })`, on a `createActionButton` labelled from `HUD_MESSAGE_KEY.securityHeldRelease`. `hud.ts` turns the intent into `dispatchCommand({ kind: 'release-guard', guardId })` and `src/main.ts` submits `{ type: 'ReleaseGuardAssignment', guardId }`.

**Those rows are the entirety of the sweep's `NEVER_LAID_OUT_WITHOUT_A_HELD_GUARD`** — three entries, all of them the same ancestor chain, differing only by the `#1`/`#2`/`#3` tie-breaker:

```
'hud > hud__rail > hud__side > ui-panel hud-staff > ui-panel__body > hud-staff__held > ' +
  'hud-staff__held-list > hud-staff__held-row > button.ui-action "Release" #1'
```

**And the sweep really does hold the clock stopped.** `aLoadedShell` ends with a Play/Pause pair and leaves the session paused; the hire block at the foot of `everyControlAt` presses `.hud-staff__hire` three times against that paused clock and dismisses all three again. So the command has a control, the control is in the sweep's inventory, and the sweep has never pressed it at any of the five viewports. **That much is exactly as reported.**

## 2. The consequence, stated plainly

`ui-pooled-rows-aim.spec.ts` proves a press on a pooled row lands on the row it is aimed at, and `ui-held-guards.spec.ts` proves the block renders — but that spec drives the panel from a synthetic `HudHeldGuardsViewModel` through the harness, not from a simulation. **Nothing anywhere measures that this button is laid out, unobscured and pressable at 375x812 in a real session.** That is the sweep's question and only the sweep's.

## 3. The recorded reason is necessary and not sufficient, and this is the correction

The constant's own comment, and #1349's entry after it, give one mechanism:

> **Hiring is not what holds a guard.** `DeploymentSystem.assignUnassignedGuards` is called from that system's `update` and from nowhere else […]; the sweep pauses the clock before its viewport loop and never restarts it […]. So three guards are hired, no system ever looks at them, all three stay `'unassigned'`, nothing claims them and `hud/held-guards` reports none

Every clause of that is true. The inference a reader draws from it — *let the clock run and the rows appear* — is **false**, and it is false for a second reason the comment does not mention.

**Measured, in a real browser, on a worktree of `7285e1c4`.** A throwaway probe: new prison, hire three guards on the Manage tab, press Play, poll the held list for up to 8 s of wall clock at ×1, press Pause.

```
[probe A] held rows with the clock paused: 0
[probe A] day progress after the run: 8%
[probe A] held rows after up to 8s of clock: 0
[probe A] staff panel held block text: ON DUTY
0 held · 3 free
Nobody is assigned right now.
A released guard stays hired and goes back to the pool.
  ✓  1 tests/browser/zz-probe.spec.ts:38:1 › A: empty prison, three hires, clock run -- does any guard become held? (33.2s)
```

**8 % of a day of real ticks, three guards on the payroll, nobody held.** The clock was not the blocker.

The blocker is issue #533 / ADR 0070 decision 1. `DeploymentSystem.requiredGuardCountFor` puts the derived sector's schedule through `resolveOccupancyScaledGuardCount`, which answers:

```ts
  if (occupantCountIsComplete && occupantCount <= 0) return 0;
```

and the derived sector is the one sector whose occupant count *is* complete (`sectorOccupantCountIsComplete`). `assignUnassignedGuards` then does `if (shortage <= 0) continue;`. **An empty prison requires zero guards, so no number of ticks claims one.** The repository already states this where it matters, in `tests/integration/security-default-sector.test.ts`:

> **Issue #533 is why this exists in six cases below that did not need it.** `resolveOccupancyScaledGuardCount` answers `0` for a sector holding nobody, so an empty prison asks for no guards and `DeploymentSystem` posts nobody -- which is the decision, not an accident. Every case that is *about* deployment therefore has to put somebody in the prison first

and that fixture's `admitOne` is what "put somebody in the prison first" costs: **wall a room perimeter, `ZoneRoom` a cell, then `AdmitPrisoner`** — because an admission into bare ground is refused `no-accommodation`.

So the true precondition list for one held `Release` row in the sweep is **five** things, not one:

1. **A walled perimeter.** `room.cell` authors `{ type: 'enclosed' }`, so a zoning without walls is refused. Measured, not assumed — a throwaway probe that skipped this step and typed `6,6,4,4` straight into the Rooms panel's coordinate fields got:

   ```
   Error: expect(locator).toHaveText(expected) failed
   Locator:  locator('[data-metric="rooms"] .ui-stat__value')
   Expected: "1"
   Received: "0"
   ```

2. **A `ZoneRoom`** through the Rooms panel.
3. **An `AdmitPrisoner`**, which is refused `no-accommodation` without step 2.
4. **A hire**, which the sweep already makes.
5. **And then** a tick that `security.deployment` is scheduled for (`schedule = { intervalTicks: 10, phaseTicks: 0 }`, so at most 10 ticks, 0.5 s at ×1).

The exemption entry's conclusion — *"with the clock this sweep runs under, the game cannot reach the state these three rows need"* — is therefore **still true, and true far more strongly than it claims**. Its stated mechanism should be corrected when the entry is next touched, because a future agent reading it will try the cheap fix, watch nothing happen, and have to rediscover #533.

## 4. Why it was not fixed here, with the measurement that decided it

The sweep is five tests, one per viewport (#1181), each `test.slow()` — a **3.0-minute cap**, which #1181 explicitly refuses to raise. The question was whether the five-step preamble in §3 fits under it.

**It does not, and the margin is not arguable.** Baseline, the unmodified part at 1280x720 on the same container the probe ran on:

```
  ✓  1 tests/browser/app-shell.spec.ts:4641:5 › the assembled application › every control can actually be pressed, on every tab at 1280x720 (#88) (2.7m)

  1 passed (2.9m)
```

**2.7 minutes against a 3.0-minute cap: about 18 seconds of headroom**, before adding anything.

And the preamble is not an 18-second thing, because of step 1. The repository already prices the wall route, in `wallRectanglesFromTheKeyboard`'s own header in the same spec file:

> **The `~3 s` is a per-press figure multiplied as though a segment were one press, and a segment is four or fourteen hops.** Measured on this container on 2026-09-08 […]: the 32 segments of the `#331` spec cost **99.0 s** […] What the wrong absolute figure hid is that this loop, not the crew, is where `test.slow()`'s allowance goes

> Measured at x4 with the clock actually running, the crew's own phase is **30.0 s for 32 segments and 22.2 s for 23**

`room.cell` authors `{ type: 'minimum-size', minWidth: 2, minHeight: 3, minTiles: 6 }`, so the smallest legal cell is **10 perimeter segments**. At the measured ~3.1 s a segment to order and ~0.95 s a segment for the crew at ×4, that is **~31 s of ordering plus ~10 s of building ≈ 40 s**, per viewport, before the zoning, the admission and the deployment tick. Against 18 s of headroom, at five viewports. The cheapest honest estimate of the change is that it roughly doubles the part that is already at 90 % of a cap #1181 refuses to raise.

**Two further risks, named because they would have to be measured and not argued even if the budget existed:**

1. **A prisoner changes the status strip.** #719 measures a fully badged strip at 1627px against 1256px of room at 1280x800, and prices the two expensive badges at **+170.5px** (`prisoners`, *"{count} with no bed"*) and **+140px** (`coverage`). An admitted prisoner with no bed lights both. The sweep asserts `payroll.unreachable` is empty at every state; a strip that overflows differently is exactly the kind of thing that turns that assertion red for a reason unrelated to the change.
2. **A running clock is not a bounded clock.** At ×1 the kernel steps 20 ticks a second (`FixedStepClock`'s 50 ms default). The deployment reconsider lands within 10 ticks, but a delivery lands 100 ticks after purchase, and `aLoadedShell` deliberately leaves nine deliveries on their way and six orders queued and asserts they are still there. One second of overshoot on a loaded runner is 20 ticks; five is the whole margin. Turning a paused sweep into one that runs the clock is a change to the thing #1181 split the test to protect.

**No exemption list was lengthened and none was shortened.** `NEVER_LAID_OUT_WITHOUT_A_HELD_GUARD` is still three entries, and `SWEEP_NEVER_PRESSES_ITS_CONTROL` still holds exactly `ReleaseGuardAssignment`.

## 5. What a fix would look like when it is taken

Two shapes, neither chosen here:

- **Inside the sweep, paid for out of it.** Add the five-step preamble to one viewport only — 1280x720 or 375x812 — so that `#1` of `NEVER_LAID_OUT_WITHOUT_A_HELD_GUARD` is laid out there. Note that the constant is shared by all five parts and `exempt` is assembled per viewport, so this is a per-viewport condition on the list rather than a deletion from it — the list falls from three to two **at that viewport**, which is still the direction it is allowed to move and never the other one. Needs the 18 s of headroom above to become real headroom first.
- **Outside the sweep, in a spec of its own.** A `ui-held-guard-release-reachable.spec.ts` on the shape of `ui-alert-dismiss-on-a-phone.spec.ts`, which is what #1201 did for the alerts fold's own unreachable-on-a-phone finding. It buys the same claim at the widths that matter without touching the sweep's budget at all — but it does **not** shorten the exemption list, because the list is about what the sweep lays out, and #1349's gate would keep its `SWEEP_NEVER_PRESSES_ITS_CONTROL` entry.

items.title: [Prisoners] Two of seven action categories have no action, so half the general-population day has nothing to do — and a riot in a prison without a yard leaves every rioter with zero legal actions
items.body:
## Context

Found by a content-reachability audit and **re-verified line by line before filing**. It is
strictly larger than #436, which asks about two *needs*; this is about two *categories* that
the regime schedules allocate a thousand ticks a day to and for which no content exists.

`ACTION_CATEGORIES` (`src/simulation/prisoners/regime.ts:1`) has **seven** members:

```ts
export const ACTION_CATEGORIES = ['sleep', 'meal', 'work', 'recreation', 'education', 'hygiene', 'free-association'] as const;
```

`DEFAULT_ACTIONS` (`src/simulation/prisoners/actions.ts:42-75`) covers **five**. Every
`category:` literal in that file, sorted and deduplicated:

```
education, hygiene, meal, recreation, sleep
```

**`work` and `free-association` have no action at all.** Not an unreachable one — none.

### What that costs a day, in a prison with an accommodation and nothing else zoned

`beginNextAction` filters `DEFAULT_ACTIONS` by the active block's `allowedCategories` and then
walks the ranked candidates (ADR 0041). Cross-referencing `GENERAL_POPULATION_REGIME` against
the eight actions:

```
  [   0, 400)  400t  sleep                             -> action.sleep
  [ 400, 500)  100t  meal/hygiene                      -> eat-in-cell, use-toilet
  [ 500,1000)  500t  work/education                    -> NONE
  [1000,1200)  200t  recreation                        -> NONE
  [1200,1300)  100t  meal                              -> eat-in-cell
  [1300,1800)  500t  work/education                    -> NONE
  [1800,2000)  200t  recreation/hygiene/free-assoc     -> use-toilet
  [2000,2100)  100t  meal                              -> eat-in-cell
  [2100,2300)  200t  recreation/free-assoc/hygiene     -> use-toilet
  [2300,2400)  100t  sleep                             -> action.sleep
```

**1,200 of 2,400 ticks a day with no resolvable action**, and 1,000 of those are the two
`work`/`education` blocks, where the only legal action is `action.classroom-education` —
which needs a zoned classroom whose furnishing costs 390 minor units. HIGH_RISK's schedule
loses 200 of 2,400.

### The riot case, which is the sharper half

`src/simulation/incidents/riot-regime.ts:12`:

```ts
export const RIOT_ALLOWED_CATEGORIES: readonly ActionCategory[] = ['free-association', 'recreation'];
```

and its comment: *"`'free-association'` (unstructured milling about) and `'recreation'` are what
remains legal: work, education, meals and scheduled hygiene all stop."*

`free-association` has no action, and both `recreation` actions target a zoned room
(`room.yard`, `room.common-room`). So **during a riot in a prison with no yard and no common
room, every rioting prisoner has zero legal resolvable actions for the whole day** and
`unmetDemandCycles` increments every cycle for every one of them. "Unstructured milling about"
names content that was never authored.

That is the shape ADR 0041 fixed for `hunger` — a prisoner whose chosen action cannot resolve
and who therefore does nothing — reappearing as an entire regime with nothing behind it.

## In scope

- Decide, per category, whether `work` and `free-association` are **unauthored content** or
  **should be dropped from `ACTION_CATEGORIES`**. This is a design decision and belongs in an
  ADR, not in implementation code (`CLAUDE.md`).
- If they are unauthored: author at least the roomless case for each, at the lower rate the
  content convention already uses (`eat-in-cell` gains 3 against `eat-meal`'s 4). A
  `free-association` action targeting `own-accommodation` with no need effect would make the
  riot regime terminate honestly even before the need question is settled.
- If they are to be dropped: the regime schedules that allocate ticks to them, and
  `RIOT_ALLOWED_CATEGORIES`, must change in the same commit — a category with no action and no
  schedule is dead type, but a schedule pointing at a dead category is a live defect.
- Either way, **the riot regime must be shown to terminate** in a prison with no yard and no
  common room.

## Out of scope

- The two *needs* with no roomless route (`hygiene`, `recreation`) — that is #436, and this
  issue should be decided in the same ADR rather than a competing one.
- Fairness / urgency ordering (#434).
- Giving a need a downstream consequence (#80, #31).
- Any save-schema change. Adding a catalogue action is content data; if that turns out to be
  false, stop and raise it (ADR 0038, #288).
- `supabase/migrations/`.

## Dependencies

- **#436** — same ADR should answer both; this issue adds the category dimension to it.
- ADR 0041 (the candidate walk this measurement assumes), ADR 0029, ADR 0032 (incident
  consequences), issue #28 (the riot regime's origin).
- **ADR number to be assigned centrally** — do not claim one.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An ADR states, per category, whether it is unauthored or should be dropped, with the
      argument.
- [ ] In a cells-only prison over a full day, **the number of ticks with no resolvable action
      is reported** before and after, from a per-action counter — not asserted.
- [ ] A riot in a prison with no yard and no common room leaves every participant with at
      least one resolvable action, or the ADR states why zero is correct and the readout says
      so.
- [ ] `ACTION_CATEGORIES` and the three schedules that consume it (`GENERAL_POPULATION_REGIME`,
      the high-risk schedule, `buildRiotRegimeSchedule`) agree: no schedule allocates ticks to
      a category with no action.
- [ ] Determinism unchanged — same population order, same candidate order, no new randomness,
      no new save key — shown, not asserted.
- [ ] `pnpm verify` green.

## Required verification

- **A green suite is not a guarded suite**: mutate any new action's `category` or target kind
  and watch a named test go red, then restore and watch it go green. Both outputs in the
  commit message.
- Run the per-action counter measurement ADR 0041 used (cell-only prison, 1 / 4 / 24
  prisoners, 24,000 ticks) and report `actions ever performed by anybody` before and after.
  The tick arithmetic above is a **static reading of two catalogues, not a run** — that is this
  issue's weakest claim and the measurement is what settles it.
- A guard that `ACTION_CATEGORIES` and `DEFAULT_ACTIONS` cannot drift apart again. The
  repository already has the shape for it: the `unconsumed-*-contract` family in
  `tests/foundation/`, with an allowlist carrying a reason per entry.

## Performance constraints

The candidate walk stops at the first resolution and `DEFAULT_ACTIONS` is small, so added
entries should be free. If a new per-category check goes inside the walk, state its cost at
`DEFAULT_PRISONER_CAPACITY`-scale population.

## Documentation impact

New ADR; `docs/SIMULATION.md` and `docs/PRISONER_OPERATIONS.md` (the action catalogue and the
regime schedules); `riot-regime.ts`'s own header comment, which currently describes behaviour
that cannot happen.

items.title: [Navigation] Implement hierarchical routing with portals, doors and security permissions
items.body:
## Context
A full-map A* per actor cannot scale to large prisons. Navigation must separate high-level chunk/sector connectivity, door/portal transitions and local grid search while respecting security classifications, lockdowns and staff-only restrictions.

## Goal
Implement the correctness foundation for hierarchical, permission-aware routing over the chunked world.

## In scope
- Navigation cell/passability projection derived from world geometry.
- Chunk/sector connectivity graph and cross-boundary portals.
- Door/gate transitions with state, direction, cost and access requirements.
- Local bounded grid search between portals/origin/destination.
- Actor route context: role, security class, permissions, escort and emergency overrides.
- Geometry/access revision invalidation signals.
- Route result structure with high-level segments and local waypoints.
- Deterministic tie-breaking and failure reasons.
- Test fixtures with cells, corridors, staff zones, secure doors and lockdown changes.

## Out of scope
- Crowd steering/local collision avoidance.
- Flow fields and shared-route optimization owned by Issue #22.
- Final path-request CPU budgets.
- Door animations or full security gameplay.
- Teleporting actors when routes fail.

## Dependencies
- Issue #12 world/chunk model.
- Issue #13 terrain/ownership/chunk decision.
- Issue #17 room/topology and geometry revisions.
- Issue #14 entity IDs/context.
.

## Architecture notes
- Global route = region/portal plan plus bounded local searches; not one unbounded tile search.
- Permission checks are part of edge traversal, not a UI-only filter.
- Caches are keyed by geometry/access versions and route context.
- Deterministic tie-breaking is required for replay/state consistency.
- A closed/locked door can invalidate connectivity without rebuilding unrelated world regions.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Routes cross chunks through explicit valid portals.
- [ ] Local search is bounded to relevant regions/segments.
- [ ] Door/security permissions produce correct allowed/denied routes.
- [ ] Lockdown/access changes invalidate affected routes/caches only.
- [ ] Identical geometry/context requests return deterministic routes.
- [ ] Unreachable destinations return structured reasons and no partial state mutation.
- [ ] Navigation imports no Phaser and does not own actor movement/rendering.
- [ ] Test layouts cover multiple route alternatives and cross-chunk doors.

## Test requirements
- Connectivity/portal construction tests.
- Door/access/lockdown matrices.
- Deterministic tie-break and cache invalidation tests.
- Cross-chunk and unreachable-route fixtures.
- Reference comparison against a small flat search for correctness on test maps.

## Performance requirements
- Record graph build/update, local search expansions and cache behavior on representative layouts.
- Budgets and large actor tiers are handled in Issue #22.

## Documentation updates
- Navigation layers, permission model, invalidation and route format.

## Definition of Done
- [ ] Correct hierarchical route generation is implemented and tested.
- [ ] Security/access rules are first-class traversal constraints.
- [ ] Downstream scheduler/movement work can consume stable route segments.

items.title: Weapons are impossible, not rare: `contraband.weapon` reads the intake tier, which cannot be 3
items.body:
Falls out of the #540 measurement ([research note](https://github.com/matmaxalez/lockstate/pull/676), comment on [#540](https://github.com/matmaxalez/lockstate/issues/540#issuecomment-5469924161)). Filed separately because it is the one finding there that reaches a player.

## The claim

`contraband.introduce` has **exactly one caller in `src/`**, and it passes the **intake** tier. `classifyPrisoner` at `priorIncidents: 0` scores `1 + 0 + 1` and clamps, so it **cannot return 3** — enumerated exhaustively over the whole intake space (77 sentence lengths × 3 screening outcomes): **63.64 / 33.33 / 3.03 / 0.00 %**, confirmed against 200,000 real draws.

The tier-3-only contraband item is therefore not rare. It is **unreachable**, and has been for as long as `ADMISSION_REQUEST` has pinned `priorIncidents: 0`.

## Why review promotion does not rescue it

Nine of the ten things gated on tier 3 *are* alive, because a review can promote a prisoner to 3 (earliest 24,000 ticks after classification; measured minimum 11.0 days). The three that are not alive all read the tier **at the classification stage** rather than the current one:

1. `contraband.weapon` — this issue.
2. The introduction probability (which caps at **0.3**, not the 0.4 recorded in #643 row 7).
3. The solitary-first intake preference.

A prisoner promoted to tier 3 on day 15 gets the high-risk regime, the route permissions, the access policy, the warning tone, the headcount and the `High` badge. They never get a weapon, because the only question ever asked about weapons was asked on the day they arrived.

## What this is not

Not a request to raise `priorIncidents`. That figure is a **recorded abstention** — `1db8c16` (#306) says of it: *"Neither number is a balance decision this file is entitled to make, so both are deliberately the least eventful values in range."* The other half of that same `as const` went #541 → #593 → ADR 0079 rather than being changed in place, and this one should go the same way if it goes anywhere. The defensive half of that commit's reasoning has already retired: `hasAccommodationTarget` now asks for every group and `DEFAULT_ACCOMMODATION_POLICY` lists both housing types for both, so a high-risk arrival can no longer reach the terminal `'failed'` stage.

## The two shapes a fix could take

- **Read the current tier where the gate is asked**, so promotion reaches all ten gates instead of seven. Cheapest, and it makes the existing review mechanic do the work it looks like it already does.
- **Decide the priors distribution**, which is a balance decision and belongs in an ADR, not in implementation code.

These are not exclusive, and the first does not require the second. Whichever way it goes, the player-visible statement today — that a high-risk prisoner may be carrying a weapon — is a promise the code does not keep.

items.title: The control that stops the payroll is enabled, in the DOM, and never on screen
items.body:
Found by playing, in the pass behind #911. **This one is not a wording question and not the owner's — it is a layout defect with a bill attached.**

## What happens

A prison with hired guards and no zoned rooms shows:

```
ON DUTY        —  0 held · 60 free
ON THE PAYROLL —  4,800 a day
```

and `.hud-staff__held-list` is **not laid out**.

Six rows exist in the DOM — three `Release` (disabled) and three `Dismiss` (**enabled**) — and all six are `visible=false`. The block draws only **assigned** guards, and a prison with no rooms has no post to assign anybody to. So every guard is `free`, no guard is `held`, and the list that would carry the dismiss control renders nothing.

## Why it matters more than a missing list usually would

The wage keeps being charged. In the run that found this, 4,800 a day against a treasury already pinned at its floor. **The one action that would stop the bleeding exists, is enabled, and cannot be reached** — and the player is told nothing about why the block is empty.

`hud.security.roster-dismiss-confirm` shipped on 2026-09-03 in the owner's own words (*"Dismiss {name}? Their wage stops and they do not come back."*). **On this prison shape that confirmation can never be reached**, so the mechanism the owner ruled on is unreachable in exactly the situation it is most needed.

## Reproduction

Fresh prison → Security tab → hire guards → do **not** zone any room → open the staff panel. `ON THE PAYROLL` climbs; the held list is not laid out; the `Dismiss` buttons are present and enabled in the DOM at `visible=false`.

Measured in `docs/research/2026-09-04-can-this-prison-fail.md` (#911). It cost that pass two full 600-second runs inside Playwright's retry loop, waiting for a control that was never going to appear. **A player gets the same, with no message.**

## What is not being claimed

That the block *should* draw unassigned guards — that is a design call about what "on duty" means, and it may well be right that the list is about posts. **The defect is that the payroll is charged for guards the panel will not show and the player cannot act on**, not that the list is filtered. Either the unassigned guards become reachable, or the panel has to say where they went; which of those is the fix is not settled here.

No player-visible wording is proposed. If the remedy needs a sentence, that sentence is the owner's under `AGENTS.md`'s fourth exclusion.

Refs #911

items.title: [Reachability] Nothing registers a security sector in a new session, so deployment, patrol, incidents and contraband search are all inert in every session a player can start
items.body:
Found while building ADR 0033's open question 3 (the release-claim command), when the #88 all-controls sweep failed for a reason bigger than the surface under test: **nothing in `src/` can hold a guard in a session a player starts.** I re-measured it independently before filing, because a finding this size is worth confirming.

## Measured

```
$ grep -rn "securitySectors.register" src/
src/simulation/runtime/session-systems.ts:587:  for (const sector of systems.security.sectorDefinitions)
                                                  runtime.securitySectors.register({ ...sector });
```

**One call site, and it is inside the restore path.** `session-systems.ts:587` is in `restoreSecuritySystems`, which reads `systems.security.sectorDefinitions` out of a save payload (written at `:512`). `src/simulation/runtime/new-session.ts` never registers a sector — `grep -n "sectorDefinitions" src/simulation/runtime/new-session.ts` is empty.

So a fresh session has **zero** `SecuritySectorDefinition`s, and a sector is the thing the rest of the tier hangs off:

- `IncidentResponseSystem` gets a responder's destination from `this.sectors.requireDefinition(incident.sectorId).postTile` (`response-system.ts:165`), and sets and clears lockdown by sector id (`:185`, `:263`).
- `alerts.ts:14,25` carry `sectorId` on every incident alert.
- `gangs.ts:77,138` resolve territory and retaliation risk by sector.
- `security-projection.ts:196` and `room-projection.ts:269` both read the sector registry for their read models.

## What this makes unreachable

The whole security and incident tier, in a session a player can start: deployment, patrol, incident response, contraband search. And by consequence, **ADR 0032's incident consequences** — the finding, the classification tier that moves, the riot that takes a prisoner from tier 0 to tier 3. All of it is measured in scenarios and restored saves, not in a session started from the front door.

**I have to correct something I reported on the strength of that.** I have been describing "an incident now costs the prisoner in it" as a thing the game does. It is a thing the *simulation* does, correctly and under test. It is not reachable from a new game, and I did not check that before saying so.

## What this does not invalidate

- **#391 and #394 are still correct and still needed.** A restored save *does* register sectors, so an interrupted incident response is reachable there — which is precisely the path #352 reported. Fixing it was not wasted; the defect was real on the path that reaches it.
- ADR 0032's mechanism is tested and sound. What is missing is the front door, not the room.

## The shape, and why it keeps happening

This is the third instance of one pattern today, and the largest:

| finding | what was unreachable | how it was found |
| --- | --- | --- |
| #287 | `GuardRoster.hire`, `SessionController.importInto` | a manual reachability audit |
| #378 | four service trees, 2,816 lines, cloud save among them | a module-graph walk from the production entries |
| this | the entire security tier in a new session | a browser sweep failing for an unrelated reason |

None of the three was caught by a gate. #369 asked for the gate and recorded why it is hard; #378 pointed out that #376 had already built the mechanism — a value-import walk from the production entries. **This instance is not that shape.** The modules here *are* in the production graph; they are imported, constructed and stepped. What is absent is a *value*: no code path supplies the data they need to do anything. A module-graph walk cannot see that.

So the gate that would catch this is different again, and probably looks like: **for each registry the composition root constructs, is there any production path that writes to it?** `securitySectors` is constructed in `new-session.ts` and written only by the restore path — that asymmetry is mechanically detectable, and it is the same asymmetry `ProcurementSystem.cancel` had before #392.

## What to decide

Not this issue's call, and ADR 0034 decision 9 puts it to the owner explicitly, but the shape of the choice:

1. **Author a default sector** (or derive one from the zoned rooms) so a new prison has somewhere a guard can be posted. Smallest path to the tier being reachable; needs a content decision about what a sector *is* when the player has not drawn one.
2. **Give the player a sector-drawing gesture**, the way zoning works. Larger, and it is the honest long-run answer if sectors are meant to be a player-facing concept at all.
3. **Decide the tier does not ship yet** and say so in the docs, which currently describe it as working.

Option 3 is the one that costs nothing today and is the most likely to rot, because five documents describe this tier's behaviour without noting that no session reaches it.

## Related

- #287, #378, #369 — the same class, and the gate discussion.
- ADR 0034 decision 9 — puts the ship/don't-ship judgement to the owner.
- #352, #391, #394 — the incident-response work this was found underneath; still valid on the restore path.

items.title: Nothing asserts that a built door is actually crossable, so the feature's headline property is unguarded
items.body:
#331 made `door-wooden` build a real door. The wiring is correct — I verified it before merging — but the property the whole change exists for is not pinned by any test.

## What is asserted, and what is not

`tests/integration/door-construction-loop.test.ts` covers the construction loop thoroughly: the order is `approved` with no door and edge `0`, then `completed` with a `DoorRegistry` row and `DOOR_EDGE_NUMERIC_ID` written; the wood plank is really spent; the door survives a save and restore at the same edge value and state; and the same command order produces byte-identical state. `tests/unit/navigation-door-and-context.test.ts` covers `checkDoorAccess` — clearance, named permissions, locks, `emergencyOverride`, and traversal-cost scaling by door state.

None of that asserts **that a prisoner can get through a wall line because there is a door in it.**

## Why that specific gap matters here

The design deliberately makes the door write into the edge layer, so `enclosure` reports a room with a door as `'sealed'` — correctly, since the perimeter really is closed. The entire reason that is safe rather than a regression is one sentence, from `definition.ts:429`:

> `DoorRegistry.getByEdge` *first* and only fall through to the wall value when …

The production code does honour it. `src/simulation/navigation/region-graph.ts:126` skips a door edge when walking region boundaries (`// door: always a region boundary`) and `src/simulation/navigation/local-search.ts:52` consults `getByEdge` for the crossing. So the behaviour is right today.

But if a later change made either of those stop consulting `DoorRegistry`, **every test added in #331 would stay green** while every door in the game silently became a wall. The construction test would still see the registry row and the edge value; the access test would still exercise `checkDoorAccess` in isolation; the determinism digests would not move, because sealing a room changes reachability rather than any hashed identifier. The failure would surface as prisoners unable to reach anything, with nothing red.

That is this repository's second documented defect class — a suite that passes regardless of correctness — applied to the newest feature rather than an old one.

## What to add

A connectivity test that fails in both directions, driven through the real construction path rather than by registering a door on `.doors` directly (a fixture that registers the door itself proves the registry, not the build):

1. Two areas separated by a complete wall line, no door: they are **two** regions and no route exists between them.
2. The same world after a `door-wooden` order completes in that wall line: they are reachable, and a prisoner actually paths across.
3. After the door is removed via #328's removal path: back to unreachable.

Case 1 is the one that makes the test real. Without it, case 2 could pass against an implementation that never sealed anything in the first place.

**Red-proof it rather than trusting it:** revert `region-graph.ts:126`'s door check, confirm the new test goes red, and quote the output. If it stays green, the test is asserting the registry rather than the crossing and needs rewriting.

## Not a defect in #331

Everything #331 shipped works. This is the guard the change is missing, filed separately so it is not lost — the merge was the right call and the coverage is the follow-up.
